Abu Lahab, the enemy of God, had stayed behind from Badr, and he sent in his place al-As ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughirah. They did this: no man stayed behind without sending another man in his place. When the news came of what had befallen the companions of Badr from Quraysh, God humiliated and disgraced him (Abu Lahab), and we felt in ourselves strength and resolve, though he (Abu Lahab) was a weak man." He said: "I used to make arrows, shaping them in the chamber of Zamzam. By God, I was sitting there shaping arrows, and with me sat Umm al-Fadl, and the news that had come had gladdened us, when the wicked Abu Lahab came dragging his feet until he sat at the edge of the chamber, with his back to my back. While he was sitting, people said: 'This is Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who has arrived.' Abu Lahab said: 'Come to me, nephew, tell me how the affair of the people went.' He said: 'Nothing, by God. It was as if, when we met them, we gave them the backs of their necks: they were killed and captured as they pleased. And by God, despite that, I did not blame the people:
We met men, white, on horses [suspended] between heaven and earth, [nothing could withstand them], and nothing could stand against them.'"
Abu Rafi' said: "I lifted the side of the chamber with my hand and then said: 'Those are the angels.' Abu Lahab raised his hand and struck my face a severe blow. I wrestled with him, and he threw me down and struck the ground with me, then he sat on me and beat me. I was a weak man. Umm al-Fadl got up, took one of the pillars of the house, and struck him a blow that split his head, a grievous wound. She said: 'Do you take advantage of him because his master is absent?' He got up and left, humiliated. By God, he did not live more than seven nights before God struck him with the 'adasah [[al-'adasah: a pustule resembling a lentil that appears on the body, of the kind of plague, which usually kills.]], and he died."
His sons left him for two or three nights without burying him, until he stank in his house. Quraysh used to avoid the 'adasah as people avoid plague. A man of Quraysh said to them: "Woe to you both! Are you not ashamed that your father has rotted in his house, and you do not wash him?" They said: "We fear this sore." He said: "Go, and we will go with you." So they did not wash him except by pouring water on him from afar, without touching him. Then they carried him and buried him at the upper part of Mecca, against a wall, and they threw stones upon him until they covered him [[Mustadrak al-Sahihayn: 3/322; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 6/89.]]."

It is narrated by Muqassam from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The one who took al-Abbas captive was Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr, brother of the Banu Salamah. Abu al-Yusr was a small, slight man, and al-Abbas was a large, heavy man. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abu al-Yusr: 'O Abu al-Yusr, how did you capture al-Abbas?'

He said: 'O Messenger of God, a man helped me against him whom I had not seen before or after, of such and such appearance.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'A noble angel helped you against him'" [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 4/103.]].

﴿ذلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ شاقُّوا اللَّهَ﴾ [That is because they opposed God]: they opposed God and His Messenger. ﴿وَمَنْ يُشاقِقِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ الْعِقابِ﴾ [And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment], meaning this is the punishment which He has hastened for you, O disbelievers. ﴿فَذُوقُوهُ﴾ [So taste it] now, ﴿وَأَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ [and that for the disbelievers] in the Hereafter ﴿عَذابَ النَّارِ﴾ [is the punishment of the Fire]. In the reading of "أن" (anna) with a fatha there are two grammatical possibilities: one is the nominative (raf'), and the other is the accusative (nasb).

As for the nominative, it is on the basis of an implied prefix: the meaning is "that (is) so, [so] taste it, for indeed the disbelievers have the punishment of the Fire."

As for the accusative, it has two aspects. The first: it is governed by an implied verb, meaning "[ذلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ] and know and be certain that [أَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ]." The second: it means "and [for] the disbelievers" – and because the preposition (yā' of the genitive, i.e., the prepositional letter) was dropped, it is put in the accusative.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 5–14 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. The commentators differ over what the particle "ka" (as) in His words ﴿ka-ma﴾ is connected to. It may be a comparison (the kaf being for comparison; see al-Qurtubi's tafsir: 7/368) with God's bringing out His Prophet from his house in truth. ʿIkrima said: the meaning is ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾, for that is better for you, just as God's bringing Muhammad out of his house in truth was good for you, even though a group of you disliked it.

Mujahid said: ﴿As your Lord brought you out, O Muhammad, from your house in truth﴾, despite the dislike of a group of the believers, so they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it; that is, they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it as they did at Badr.

Some said: God commanded His Messenger, peace be upon him, to proceed with his command regarding the spoils despite the dislike of some of his companions, just as he proceeded with his command when he set out from his house to pursue the caravan while they were unwilling.

It was said: its meaning is ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ with disputation, just as they disputed with you on the day of Badr when they said: You brought us out for the caravan and did not inform us of fighting [so we would be displeased].

It was said: its meaning is ﴿Those are the true believers﴾ ﴿as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾.

Some said: the kaf means "upon"; its implied sense is: proceed upon that to which your Lord brought you out.

Ibn Hayyan said, from al-Kalbi: Abu ʿUbayda said it means an oath, its sense being: By Him who brought you out of your house in truth. It was also said: the kaf means "when," its implied sense being: When your Lord brought you out of your house in Medina to Badr in truth. [See Ibn al-Jawzi's Zad al-Masir: 3/218.]

﴿Indeed, a group of the believers were averse﴾ to the pursuit of the polytheists. ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth﴾, that is, concerning the fighting. This was because when the believers became certain of the armed strength and of war on the day of Badr, and understood that it was fighting, they disliked it and said: O Messenger of God, you did not inform us that we would meet the enemy so that we might prepare for battle; we only went out for the caravan. This is their dispute, ﴿after it had become clear to them﴾ that you do nothing except what God has commanded.

Ibn Zayd said: these are the polytheists who dispute with him concerning the truth, ﴿as if they were being driven to death﴾, meaning those who are called to Islam, because of their aversion to it, ﴿while they look on﴾.

﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾. The verse.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Yasar and al-Suddi said: Kurz ibn Jabir al-Qurashi raided the pasture of Medina until he reached al-Safra. The Prophet ﷺ was informed, so he rode in pursuit, but Kurz outpaced him, and the Prophet ﷺ returned and remained for a year. Abu Sufyan had come from Syria with a caravan of Quraysh in which were ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿAmr ibn Hisham, and Makhrama ibn Nawfal al-Zuhri, with forty riders from the nobles of Quraysh, and in it was great merchandise, namely the luggage caravan. When he was near Badr, the Prophet ﷺ received word, so he summoned his companions against them and informed them of the abundance of wealth and the scarcity of troops, saying: "This is the caravan of Quraysh, in which is their property; go out to it, perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will grant it to you as spoil." [216] They set out, intending only Abu Sufyan, and the riders did not regard it except as a spoil for themselves; some hastened and some were reluctant.

This was because they had not supposed that the Messenger of God ﷺ would meet battle. When Abu Sufyan heard of the Prophet's ﷺ march, he hired Damdam ibn ʿAmr al-Ghifari and sent him to Mecca, ordering him to come to Quraysh, call them to arms, and inform them that Muhammad had intercepted their caravan with his companions.

Damdam set out quickly for Mecca, and Satan went out with him in the form of Suraqa ibn Khatham. He came to Mecca and said: "Muhammad and his companions have intercepted your caravan. ﴿There is no one who can overcome you today among the people, and I am your protector﴾." The people of Mecca grew angry and rallied, calling out: "None of us shall stay behind; whoever does, we will demolish his house and plunder him." The Messenger of God ﷺ went out with his companions until he reached a valley called Wafran, and news reached him of Quraysh's march to protect their caravan. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, set out until, when they were at al-Ruha, he took a spy from the people, who informed him of them. The Messenger of God ﷺ also sent a spy of his own from Juhayna, an ally of the Ansar, named Ibn al-Uraiqit, who brought him news of the people. The caravan outran the Messenger of God ﷺ, and Gabriel descended and said: "God has promised you ﴿one of the two groups﴾, either the caravan or Quraysh." They preferred the caravan. The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions about pursuing the caravan or fighting the army. Abu Bakr stood and spoke well; ʿUmar stood and spoke well. Then al-Miqdad ibn ʿAmr stood and said: "O Messenger of God, proceed as God has commanded you, and we are with you. By God, we will not say as the children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 24]; rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight, and we are fighting with you. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us to Bark al-ʿImad, we would fight alongside you until we reached it."

The Messenger of God ﷺ said good things to him and prayed good for him. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Advise me, O people." [217]

He meant the Ansar, for when they pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqaba they had said: "O Messenger of God, we are free of your covenant until you reach our homes; when you reach our dwellings, you are under our protection, and we will defend you as we defend our sons and women." The Messenger of God ﷺ feared that the Ansar would not consider it incumbent upon them to support him except against one who attacked him in Medina, and that it was not incumbent upon them to send him to their enemy beyond their lands. When the Messenger of God ﷺ said that, Saʿd ibn Muʿadh said to him: "By God, it seems you mean us, O Messenger of God?"

He ﷺ said: "Indeed."

He said: "We have believed in you and confirmed you, and we testify that what you have brought is the truth, and we have given you our pledges and covenants of hearing and obedience. So proceed, O Messenger of God, with what you desire. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge in with you; not one man of us would stay behind. We do not dislike that our enemy should meet us with us tomorrow; we are steadfast in war and truthful at the encounter. Perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will show you from us what will delight your eye. So march with us in God's blessing."

The Prophet ﷺ was delighted by that, and Saʿd's words invigorated him. Then he said: "Proceed in God's blessing and rejoice, for God has promised you one of the two groups. By God, I am now looking at the places where the people will fall." [Fully, dispersed, in al-Tabari's tafsir: 9/145, 248, and Bayhaqi's Dala'il: 3/110.]

That is His words: ﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾, that is, of the two parties: one was Abu Sufyan with the caravan, and the other was Abu Jahl with the army. ﴿And you wished that the unarmed one would be yours﴾, meaning the caravan in which there was no fighting. ﴿Shawka﴾ is strength and power, and its root is from thorn (shawk). ﴿But God wills to establish the truth﴾, that is, to confirm it and make it manifest, ﴿by His words﴾, by His command to you to fight the unbelievers, ﴿and to cut off the last of the disbelievers﴾, so that He may uproot them, ﴿that He might establish the truth﴾, Islam, ﴿and nullify falsehood﴾, disbelief.

It was said: the truth is the Qur'an and falsehood is Satan. ﴿Though the guilty disliked it﴾, that is, the polytheists.

﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾, that is, sought refuge in Him from your enemy and asked Him for victory over them.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: On the day of Badr, when the Messenger of God ﷺ saw the multitude of polytheists and the scarcity of Muslims, he entered the tent, he and Abu Bakr, faced the qibla, and began to supplicate, saying: "O God, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O God, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on earth." He continued thus until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr took his cloak, placed it on his shoulders, embraced him from behind, and said: "O Prophet of God, enough of your entreating your Lord, for God will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you."

﴿So He answered you: "I will reinforce you﴾, that is, that I. ʿIsa read it with a kasra on the alif, "innī," and said: "Indeed I am reinforcing you and adding to you and sending aid to you ﴿with a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾." The people of Medina read ﴿murdifīn﴾ with a fatha on the dal, and the rest with a kasra; both are dialects meaning successive, following one another. It is said: "ardafahu" and "radafahu" both mean "to follow him." The poet said:

"When the Jawza' follows the Thurayya, I suspect the family of Fatima of suspicions" [Taj al-ʿArus: 6/115; Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/245].

He meant: "radafat" — came after it, because the Jawza' rises after the Thurayya. Whoever reads with a fatha, it is in the passive sense, meaning God reinforced the Muslims and brought it to them, and God reinforced them with angels. Gabriel descended with five hundred angels on the right wing, among whom was Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him; Michael descended with five hundred on the left, among whom was ʿAli, may God ennoble his face. They were in the form of men, wearing white garments and white turbans, their ends hanging between their shoulders. The angels fought on the day of Badr; they did not fight on the day of the Confederates, nor on the day of Hunayn, and they never fight except as reinforcements or as aid.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: While a man from the Muslims was running after a man from the polytheists, he heard a lash strike above him and the voice of a horseman saying: "Advance, Hayzum!" He looked at the polytheist ahead of him, who fell on his back; he looked at him, and his face was split and cut like the stroke of a whip. The man came and related this to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "You have spoken truly; that is from the reinforcement of heaven." That day they killed seventy and captured seventy. [218]

Mujahid said: The Prophet ﷺ was not reinforced, as God mentioned, except by the thousand of the angels ﴿following one another﴾ mentioned in al-Anfal; as for three thousand and five thousand, they were glad tidings.

﴿And God did not make it except as good news﴾, meaning the reinforcement.

al-Farra': meaning the reinforcements.

﴿And that your hearts might be reassured thereby. Victory is only from God. Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿When He covered you with drowsiness as security from Him﴾. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿yaghshikum﴾ with a fatha on the ya, with ﴿al-nuʿas﴾ in the nominative, taking the verb as having it as its subject, citing His words in Surat Al ʿImran: ﴿security, drowsiness overcoming a group of you﴾ [Surat Al ʿImran: 154], making the verb belong to it.

The people of Medina read ﴿yughshikum﴾ with a damma on the ya and lightened, taking the verb as God's, so that it would agree with His words ﴿and He sends down﴾ and ﴿and to purify you﴾; they cited His words, "as if their faces had been covered" [Surat Yunus: 27].

ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', ʿIkrima, al-Jahdari, ʿIsa, and the people of Kufa read ﴿yughashshikum﴾ with a damma on the ya and a shadda.

Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, citing His words ﴿and it covered what it covered﴾ [Surat al-Najm: 54]. "Al-nuʿas" is sleep, lightened. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the beginning of the people's... ﴿amanatan﴾ with a fatha on the mim is the reading of the common people; Abu Hayat and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿amnatan﴾ with a sukun on the mim, which is the verbal noun of your saying "amintu min kadha, amanan, amanatan, wa amanatan," all meaning the same, which is why it is in the accusative.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud said: Drowsiness in battle is security from God, mighty and majestic, and in prayer it is from Satan.

﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky﴾. This was because the Muslims had alighted at a green sand dune at Badr, into which the foot and the hooves of animals sink, while the polytheists had preceded them to the water of Badr al-ʿUzma and had taken control of it. In the morning some of the Muslims were in a state of minor impurity and some of major impurity; thirst afflicted them, and Satan whispered to them: "You claim that the Prophet of God is among you and that you are the friends of God, yet the polytheists have overcome you at the water, and you pray in impurity, minor and major. How, then, do you hope to triumph over them?"

He said: God, mighty and majestic, sent rain, from which the valley flowed; the believers drank from it, bathed, performed ablution, watered the mounts, and filled the water-skins. The dust settled, the ground was packed so that feet were firmly planted, the whisperings of Satan ceased, and their souls were content. This is His words: ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby﴾, from minor and major impurity.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read ﴿liyutahhirakum﴾ with a quiet ta' from "atharahu Allah," [purify].

﴿And to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾, that is, the whisper of Satan.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿rujzu﴾ with a damma on the ra'. Abu al-ʿAliya read ﴿rijs﴾ with a sin, as the Arabs interchange sin and zay, saying "bazaq" and "basaq."

"Al-sirat" and "al-zirat," "al-asad" and "al-azd."

﴿And to bind your hearts﴾ with certainty and patience, ﴿and to make firm the feet﴾, so that they do not slip in the sand, by packing the ground.

It was said: by patience and strength of heart.

﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you, so make firm those who believe"﴾, that is, with help and victory; so make firm those who believe, that is, illuminate their hearts, correct their resolve and their steadfastness in jihad. It was said: that making firm was by their presence with them in the battle.

It was said: their aid to them against their enemy. Abu Rawq said: the angel would appear in the form of a man whom they recognized; he would come to one of the Prophet's companions and say: "I have drawn near the polytheists and heard them say, 'By God, if they charge against us, we will surely [break them]'." The Muslims would then relate this to one another, which strengthened their souls and increased their boldness.

Ibn Ishaq and al-Mubarrad said: ﴿So make firm those who believe﴾, that is, support them. ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾. Then He taught them how to strike and kill, saying: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾.

Some said: this command is connected to His words, "so make firm those who believe."

Others said: it is a command from God, mighty and majestic, to the believers. They differed over His words ﴿above the necks﴾. ʿAtiyya and al-Dahhak said: it means strike the necks, as in His words ﴿when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾ [Surat Muhammad: 4].

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I was not sent to punish with the punishment of God, but I was sent to strike necks and to tighten bonds." [219]

Some said: it means "strike upon the necks," with "fawq" meaning "upon." ʿIkrima said: it means strike the heads above the necks. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means strike above the necks, that is, upon the necks; its parallel is His words ﴿if they are women above two﴾ [Surat al-Nisa': 11], meaning two or more than two.

﴿And strike from them every fingertip﴾. ʿAtiyya said: that is, every joint.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak said: it means the extremities; "banan" is the plural of "bananah," which are the tips of the fingers of the hands and feet, and its derivation is from "abana bi'l-maqam" when one stays in a place.

The poet said:

"Would that I had cut off his fingertip, and met him in the house, awake and wary" [The line is by ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas, as in Lisan al-ʿArab: 13/59].

Yaman ibn Ra'ab said: ﴿strike above the necks﴾ means the chieftains, and ﴿strike from them every fingertip﴾ means the lowly. The correct view is the first. Abu Dawud al-Mazini, who had witnessed Badr, said: I pursued a man from the polytheists to strike him on the day of Badr; his head fell before my sword reached him, so I knew that someone else had killed him.

Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf narrated from his father, who said: I saw on the day of Badr that one of us would point his sword at a polytheist, and his head would fall from his body before the sword reached him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: a man from the tribe of Ghifar told me: My cousin and I came and climbed a mountain to overlook Badr, and we were polytheists awaiting the outcome, to see on whom the defeat would fall, so we could plunder with the plunderers.

He said: While we were on the mountain, a cloud drew near us, and we heard in it the neighing of horses, and I heard a speaker say: "Advance, Hayzum!" [Hayzum was the name of Gabriel's horse.] As for my cousin, the veil over his heart was lifted and he died; as for me, I nearly perished, then I steadied myself.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 5–14 (part 2 of 2):

Ikrimah said: Abu Rafi', the freedman of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), said: "I was a slave of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and Islam had entered our household: Umm al-Fadl had embraced Islam, and I had embraced it too. But al-Abbas used to fear his people and disliked opposing them, so he concealed his Islam. He was a man of great wealth, dispersed among his people. Abu Lahab, the enemy of God, had stayed behind from Badr, and he sent in his place al-As ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughirah. They did this: no man stayed behind without sending another man in his place. When the news came of what had befallen the companions of Badr from Quraysh, God humiliated and disgraced him (Abu Lahab), and we felt in ourselves strength and resolve, though he (Abu Lahab) was a weak man." He said: "I used to make arrows, shaping them in the chamber of Zamzam. By God, I was sitting there shaping arrows, and with me sat Umm al-Fadl, and the news that had come had gladdened us, when the wicked Abu Lahab came dragging his feet until he sat at the edge of the chamber, with his back to my back. While he was sitting, people said: 'This is Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who has arrived.' Abu Lahab said: 'Come to me, nephew, tell me how the affair of the people went.' He said: 'Nothing, by God. It was as if, when we met them, we gave them the backs of their necks: they were killed and captured as they pleased. And by God, despite that, I did not blame the people:
We met men, white, on horses [suspended] between heaven and earth, [nothing could withstand them], and nothing could stand against them.'"
Abu Rafi' said: "I lifted the side of the chamber with my hand and then said: 'Those are the angels.' Abu Lahab raised his hand and struck my face a severe blow. I wrestled with him, and he threw me down and struck the ground with me, then he sat on me and beat me. I was a weak man. Umm al-Fadl got up, took one of the pillars of the house, and struck him a blow that split his head, a grievous wound. She said: 'Do you take advantage of him because his master is absent?' He got up and left, humiliated. By God, he did not live more than seven nights before God struck him with the 'adasah [[al-'adasah: a pustule resembling a lentil that appears on the body, of the kind of plague, which usually kills.]], and he died."
His sons left him for two or three nights without burying him, until he stank in his house. Quraysh used to avoid the 'adasah as people avoid plague. A man of Quraysh said to them: "Woe to you both! Are you not ashamed that your father has rotted in his house, and you do not wash him?" They said: "We fear this sore." He said: "Go, and we will go with you." So they did not wash him except by pouring water on him from afar, without touching him. Then they carried him and buried him at the upper part of Mecca, against a wall, and they threw stones upon him until they covered him [[Mustadrak al-Sahihayn: 3/322; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 6/89.]]."

It is narrated by Muqassam from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The one who took al-Abbas captive was Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr, brother of the Banu Salamah. Abu al-Yusr was a small, slight man, and al-Abbas was a large, heavy man. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abu al-Yusr: 'O Abu al-Yusr, how did you capture al-Abbas?'

He said: 'O Messenger of God, a man helped me against him whom I had not seen before or after, of such and such appearance.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'A noble angel helped you against him'" [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 4/103.]].

﴿ذلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ شاقُّوا اللَّهَ﴾ [That is because they opposed God]: they opposed God and His Messenger. ﴿وَمَنْ يُشاقِقِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ الْعِقابِ﴾ [And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment], meaning this is the punishment which He has hastened for you, O disbelievers. ﴿فَذُوقُوهُ﴾ [So taste it] now, ﴿وَأَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ [and that for the disbelievers] in the Hereafter ﴿عَذابَ النَّارِ﴾ [is the punishment of the Fire]. In the reading of "أن" (anna) with a fatha there are two grammatical possibilities: one is the nominative (raf'), and the other is the accusative (nasb).

As for the nominative, it is on the basis of an implied prefix: the meaning is "that (is) so, [so] taste it, for indeed the disbelievers have the punishment of the Fire."

As for the accusative, it has two aspects. The first: it is governed by an implied verb, meaning "[ذلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ] and know and be certain that [أَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ]." The second: it means "and [for] the disbelievers" – and because the preposition (yā' of the genitive, i.e., the prepositional letter) was dropped, it is put in the accusative.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 5–14 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. The commentators differ over what the particle "ka" (as) in His words ﴿ka-ma﴾ is connected to. It may be a comparison (the kaf being for comparison; see al-Qurtubi's tafsir: 7/368) with God's bringing out His Prophet from his house in truth. ʿIkrima said: the meaning is ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾, for that is better for you, just as God's bringing Muhammad out of his house in truth was good for you, even though a group of you disliked it.

Mujahid said: ﴿As your Lord brought you out, O Muhammad, from your house in truth﴾, despite the dislike of a group of the believers, so they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it; that is, they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it as they did at Badr.

Some said: God commanded His Messenger, peace be upon him, to proceed with his command regarding the spoils despite the dislike of some of his companions, just as he proceeded with his command when he set out from his house to pursue the caravan while they were unwilling.

It was said: its meaning is ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ with disputation, just as they disputed with you on the day of Badr when they said: You brought us out for the caravan and did not inform us of fighting [so we would be displeased].

It was said: its meaning is ﴿Those are the true believers﴾ ﴿as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾.

Some said: the kaf means "upon"; its implied sense is: proceed upon that to which your Lord brought you out.

Ibn Hayyan said, from al-Kalbi: Abu ʿUbayda said it means an oath, its sense being: By Him who brought you out of your house in truth. It was also said: the kaf means "when," its implied sense being: When your Lord brought you out of your house in Medina to Badr in truth. [See Ibn al-Jawzi's Zad al-Masir: 3/218.]

﴿Indeed, a group of the believers were averse﴾ to the pursuit of the polytheists. ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth﴾, that is, concerning the fighting. This was because when the believers became certain of the armed strength and of war on the day of Badr, and understood that it was fighting, they disliked it and said: O Messenger of God, you did not inform us that we would meet the enemy so that we might prepare for battle; we only went out for the caravan. This is their dispute, ﴿after it had become clear to them﴾ that you do nothing except what God has commanded.

Ibn Zayd said: these are the polytheists who dispute with him concerning the truth, ﴿as if they were being driven to death﴾, meaning those who are called to Islam, because of their aversion to it, ﴿while they look on﴾.

﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾. The verse.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Yasar and al-Suddi said: Kurz ibn Jabir al-Qurashi raided the pasture of Medina until he reached al-Safra. The Prophet ﷺ was informed, so he rode in pursuit, but Kurz outpaced him, and the Prophet ﷺ returned and remained for a year. Abu Sufyan had come from Syria with a caravan of Quraysh in which were ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿAmr ibn Hisham, and Makhrama ibn Nawfal al-Zuhri, with forty riders from the nobles of Quraysh, and in it was great merchandise, namely the luggage caravan. When he was near Badr, the Prophet ﷺ received word, so he summoned his companions against them and informed them of the abundance of wealth and the scarcity of troops, saying: "This is the caravan of Quraysh, in which is their property; go out to it, perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will grant it to you as spoil." [216] They set out, intending only Abu Sufyan, and the riders did not regard it except as a spoil for themselves; some hastened and some were reluctant.

This was because they had not supposed that the Messenger of God ﷺ would meet battle. When Abu Sufyan heard of the Prophet's ﷺ march, he hired Damdam ibn ʿAmr al-Ghifari and sent him to Mecca, ordering him to come to Quraysh, call them to arms, and inform them that Muhammad had intercepted their caravan with his companions.

Damdam set out quickly for Mecca, and Satan went out with him in the form of Suraqa ibn Khatham. He came to Mecca and said: "Muhammad and his companions have intercepted your caravan. ﴿There is no one who can overcome you today among the people, and I am your protector﴾." The people of Mecca grew angry and rallied, calling out: "None of us shall stay behind; whoever does, we will demolish his house and plunder him." The Messenger of God ﷺ went out with his companions until he reached a valley called Wafran, and news reached him of Quraysh's march to protect their caravan. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, set out until, when they were at al-Ruha, he took a spy from the people, who informed him of them. The Messenger of God ﷺ also sent a spy of his own from Juhayna, an ally of the Ansar, named Ibn al-Uraiqit, who brought him news of the people. The caravan outran the Messenger of God ﷺ, and Gabriel descended and said: "God has promised you ﴿one of the two groups﴾, either the caravan or Quraysh." They preferred the caravan. The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions about pursuing the caravan or fighting the army. Abu Bakr stood and spoke well; ʿUmar stood and spoke well. Then al-Miqdad ibn ʿAmr stood and said: "O Messenger of God, proceed as God has commanded you, and we are with you. By God, we will not say as the children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 24]; rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight, and we are fighting with you. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us to Bark al-ʿImad, we would fight alongside you until we reached it."

The Messenger of God ﷺ said good things to him and prayed good for him. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Advise me, O people." [217]

He meant the Ansar, for when they pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqaba they had said: "O Messenger of God, we are free of your covenant until you reach our homes; when you reach our dwellings, you are under our protection, and we will defend you as we defend our sons and women." The Messenger of God ﷺ feared that the Ansar would not consider it incumbent upon them to support him except against one who attacked him in Medina, and that it was not incumbent upon them to send him to their enemy beyond their lands. When the Messenger of God ﷺ said that, Saʿd ibn Muʿadh said to him: "By God, it seems you mean us, O Messenger of God?"

He ﷺ said: "Indeed."

He said: "We have believed in you and confirmed you, and we testify that what you have brought is the truth, and we have given you our pledges and covenants of hearing and obedience. So proceed, O Messenger of God, with what you desire. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge in with you; not one man of us would stay behind. We do not dislike that our enemy should meet us with us tomorrow; we are steadfast in war and truthful at the encounter. Perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will show you from us what will delight your eye. So march with us in God's blessing."

The Prophet ﷺ was delighted by that, and Saʿd's words invigorated him. Then he said: "Proceed in God's blessing and rejoice, for God has promised you one of the two groups. By God, I am now looking at the places where the people will fall." [Fully, dispersed, in al-Tabari's tafsir: 9/145, 248, and Bayhaqi's Dala'il: 3/110.]

That is His words: ﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾, that is, of the two parties: one was Abu Sufyan with the caravan, and the other was Abu Jahl with the army. ﴿And you wished that the unarmed one would be yours﴾, meaning the caravan in which there was no fighting. ﴿Shawka﴾ is strength and power, and its root is from thorn (shawk). ﴿But God wills to establish the truth﴾, that is, to confirm it and make it manifest, ﴿by His words﴾, by His command to you to fight the unbelievers, ﴿and to cut off the last of the disbelievers﴾, so that He may uproot them, ﴿that He might establish the truth﴾, Islam, ﴿and nullify falsehood﴾, disbelief.

It was said: the truth is the Qur'an and falsehood is Satan. ﴿Though the guilty disliked it﴾, that is, the polytheists.

﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾, that is, sought refuge in Him from your enemy and asked Him for victory over them.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: On the day of Badr, when the Messenger of God ﷺ saw the multitude of polytheists and the scarcity of Muslims, he entered the tent, he and Abu Bakr, faced the qibla, and began to supplicate, saying: "O God, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O God, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on earth." He continued thus until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr took his cloak, placed it on his shoulders, embraced him from behind, and said: "O Prophet of God, enough of your entreating your Lord, for God will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you."

﴿So He answered you: "I will reinforce you﴾, that is, that I. ʿIsa read it with a kasra on the alif, "innī," and said: "Indeed I am reinforcing you and adding to you and sending aid to you ﴿with a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾." The people of Medina read ﴿murdifīn﴾ with a fatha on the dal, and the rest with a kasra; both are dialects meaning successive, following one another. It is said: "ardafahu" and "radafahu" both mean "to follow him." The poet said:

"When the Jawza' follows the Thurayya, I suspect the family of Fatima of suspicions" [Taj al-ʿArus: 6/115; Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/245].

He meant: "radafat" — came after it, because the Jawza' rises after the Thurayya. Whoever reads with a fatha, it is in the passive sense, meaning God reinforced the Muslims and brought it to them, and God reinforced them with angels. Gabriel descended with five hundred angels on the right wing, among whom was Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him; Michael descended with five hundred on the left, among whom was ʿAli, may God ennoble his face. They were in the form of men, wearing white garments and white turbans, their ends hanging between their shoulders. The angels fought on the day of Badr; they did not fight on the day of the Confederates, nor on the day of Hunayn, and they never fight except as reinforcements or as aid.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: While a man from the Muslims was running after a man from the polytheists, he heard a lash strike above him and the voice of a horseman saying: "Advance, Hayzum!" He looked at the polytheist ahead of him, who fell on his back; he looked at him, and his face was split and cut like the stroke of a whip. The man came and related this to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "You have spoken truly; that is from the reinforcement of heaven." That day they killed seventy and captured seventy. [218]

Mujahid said: The Prophet ﷺ was not reinforced, as God mentioned, except by the thousand of the angels ﴿following one another﴾ mentioned in al-Anfal; as for three thousand and five thousand, they were glad tidings.

﴿And God did not make it except as good news﴾, meaning the reinforcement.

al-Farra': meaning the reinforcements.

﴿And that your hearts might be reassured thereby. Victory is only from God. Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿When He covered you with drowsiness as security from Him﴾. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿yaghshikum﴾ with a fatha on the ya, with ﴿al-nuʿas﴾ in the nominative, taking the verb as having it as its subject, citing His words in Surat Al ʿImran: ﴿security, drowsiness overcoming a group of you﴾ [Surat Al ʿImran: 154], making the verb belong to it.

The people of Medina read ﴿yughshikum﴾ with a damma on the ya and lightened, taking the verb as God's, so that it would agree with His words ﴿and He sends down﴾ and ﴿and to purify you﴾; they cited His words, "as if their faces had been covered" [Surat Yunus: 27].

ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', ʿIkrima, al-Jahdari, ʿIsa, and the people of Kufa read ﴿yughashshikum﴾ with a damma on the ya and a shadda.

Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, citing His words ﴿and it covered what it covered﴾ [Surat al-Najm: 54]. "Al-nuʿas" is sleep, lightened. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the beginning of the people's... ﴿amanatan﴾ with a fatha on the mim is the reading of the common people; Abu Hayat and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿amnatan﴾ with a sukun on the mim, which is the verbal noun of your saying "amintu min kadha, amanan, amanatan, wa amanatan," all meaning the same, which is why it is in the accusative.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud said: Drowsiness in battle is security from God, mighty and majestic, and in prayer it is from Satan.

﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky﴾. This was because the Muslims had alighted at a green sand dune at Badr, into which the foot and the hooves of animals sink, while the polytheists had preceded them to the water of Badr al-ʿUzma and had taken control of it. In the morning some of the Muslims were in a state of minor impurity and some of major impurity; thirst afflicted them, and Satan whispered to them: "You claim that the Prophet of God is among you and that you are the friends of God, yet the polytheists have overcome you at the water, and you pray in impurity, minor and major. How, then, do you hope to triumph over them?"

He said: God, mighty and majestic, sent rain, from which the valley flowed; the believers drank from it, bathed, performed ablution, watered the mounts, and filled the water-skins. The dust settled, the ground was packed so that feet were firmly planted, the whisperings of Satan ceased, and their souls were content. This is His words: ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby﴾, from minor and major impurity.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read ﴿liyutahhirakum﴾ with a quiet ta' from "atharahu Allah," [purify].

﴿And to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾, that is, the whisper of Satan.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿rujzu﴾ with a damma on the ra'. Abu al-ʿAliya read ﴿rijs﴾ with a sin, as the Arabs interchange sin and zay, saying "bazaq" and "basaq."

"Al-sirat" and "al-zirat," "al-asad" and "al-azd."

﴿And to bind your hearts﴾ with certainty and patience, ﴿and to make firm the feet﴾, so that they do not slip in the sand, by packing the ground.

It was said: by patience and strength of heart.

﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you, so make firm those who believe"﴾, that is, with help and victory; so make firm those who believe, that is, illuminate their hearts, correct their resolve and their steadfastness in jihad. It was said: that making firm was by their presence with them in the battle.

It was said: their aid to them against their enemy. Abu Rawq said: the angel would appear in the form of a man whom they recognized; he would come to one of the Prophet's companions and say: "I have drawn near the polytheists and heard them say, 'By God, if they charge against us, we will surely [break them]'." The Muslims would then relate this to one another, which strengthened their souls and increased their boldness.

Ibn Ishaq and al-Mubarrad said: ﴿So make firm those who believe﴾, that is, support them. ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾. Then He taught them how to strike and kill, saying: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾.

Some said: this command is connected to His words, "so make firm those who believe."

Others said: it is a command from God, mighty and majestic, to the believers. They differed over His words ﴿above the necks﴾. ʿAtiyya and al-Dahhak said: it means strike the necks, as in His words ﴿when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾ [Surat Muhammad: 4].

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I was not sent to punish with the punishment of God, but I was sent to strike necks and to tighten bonds." [219]

Some said: it means "strike upon the necks," with "fawq" meaning "upon." ʿIkrima said: it means strike the heads above the necks. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means strike above the necks, that is, upon the necks; its parallel is His words ﴿if they are women above two﴾ [Surat al-Nisa': 11], meaning two or more than two.

﴿And strike from them every fingertip﴾. ʿAtiyya said: that is, every joint.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak said: it means the extremities; "banan" is the plural of "bananah," which are the tips of the fingers of the hands and feet, and its derivation is from "abana bi'l-maqam" when one stays in a place.

The poet said:

"Would that I had cut off his fingertip, and met him in the house, awake and wary" [The line is by ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas, as in Lisan al-ʿArab: 13/59].

Yaman ibn Ra'ab said: ﴿strike above the necks﴾ means the chieftains, and ﴿strike from them every fingertip﴾ means the lowly. The correct view is the first. Abu Dawud al-Mazini, who had witnessed Badr, said: I pursued a man from the polytheists to strike him on the day of Badr; his head fell before my sword reached him, so I knew that someone else had killed him.

Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf narrated from his father, who said: I saw on the day of Badr that one of us would point his sword at a polytheist, and his head would fall from his body before the sword reached him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: a man from the tribe of Ghifar told me: My cousin and I came and climbed a mountain to overlook Badr, and we were polytheists awaiting the outcome, to see on whom the defeat would fall, so we could plunder with the plunderers.

He said: While we were on the mountain, a cloud drew near us, and we heard in it the neighing of horses, and I heard a speaker say: "Advance, Hayzum!" [Hayzum was the name of Gabriel's horse.] As for my cousin, the veil over his heart was lifted and he died; as for me, I nearly perished, then I steadied myself.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 5–14 (part 2 of 2):

Ikrimah said: Abu Rafi', the freedman of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), said: "I was a slave of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and Islam had entered our household: Umm al-Fadl had embraced Islam, and I had embraced it too. But al-Abbas used to fear his people and disliked opposing them, so he concealed his Islam. He was a man of great wealth, dispersed among his people. Abu Lahab, the enemy of God, had stayed behind from Badr, and he sent in his place al-As ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughirah. They did this: no man stayed behind without sending another man in his place. When the news came of what had befallen the companions of Badr from Quraysh, God humiliated and disgraced him (Abu Lahab), and we felt in ourselves strength and resolve, though he (Abu Lahab) was a weak man." He said: "I used to make arrows, shaping them in the chamber of Zamzam. By God, I was sitting there shaping arrows, and with me sat Umm al-Fadl, and the news that had come had gladdened us, when the wicked Abu Lahab came dragging his feet until he sat at the edge of the chamber, with his back to my back. While he was sitting, people said: 'This is Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who has arrived.' Abu Lahab said: 'Come to me, nephew, tell me how the affair of the people went.' He said: 'Nothing, by God. It was as if, when we met them, we gave them the backs of their necks: they were killed and captured as they pleased. And by God, despite that, I did not blame the people:
We met men, white, on horses [suspended] between heaven and earth, [nothing could withstand them], and nothing could stand against them.'"
Abu Rafi' said: "I lifted the side of the chamber with my hand and then said: 'Those are the angels.' Abu Lahab raised his hand and struck my face a severe blow. I wrestled with him, and he threw me down and struck the ground with me, then he sat on me and beat me. I was a weak man. Umm al-Fadl got up, took one of the pillars of the house, and struck him a blow that split his head, a grievous wound. She said: 'Do you take advantage of him because his master is absent?' He got up and left, humiliated. By God, he did not live more than seven nights before God struck him with the 'adasah [[al-'adasah: a pustule resembling a lentil that appears on the body, of the kind of plague, which usually kills.]], and he died."
His sons left him for two or three nights without burying him, until he stank in his house. Quraysh used to avoid the 'adasah as people avoid plague. A man of Quraysh said to them: "Woe to you both! Are you not ashamed that your father has rotted in his house, and you do not wash him?" They said: "We fear this sore." He said: "Go, and we will go with you." So they did not wash him except by pouring water on him from afar, without touching him. Then they carried him and buried him at the upper part of Mecca, against a wall, and they threw stones upon him until they covered him [[Mustadrak al-Sahihayn: 3/322; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 6/89.]]."

It is narrated by Muqassam from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The one who took al-Abbas captive was Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr, brother of the Banu Salamah. Abu al-Yusr was a small, slight man, and al-Abbas was a large, heavy man. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abu al-Yusr: 'O Abu al-Yusr, how did you capture al-Abbas?'

He said: 'O Messenger of God, a man helped me against him whom I had not seen before or after, of such and such appearance.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'A noble angel helped you against him'" [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 4/103.]].

﴿ذلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ شاقُّوا اللَّهَ﴾ [That is because they opposed God]: they opposed God and His Messenger. ﴿وَمَنْ يُشاقِقِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ الْعِقابِ﴾ [And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment], meaning this is the punishment which He has hastened for you, O disbelievers. ﴿فَذُوقُوهُ﴾ [So taste it] now, ﴿وَأَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ [and that for the disbelievers] in the Hereafter ﴿عَذابَ النَّارِ﴾ [is the punishment of the Fire]. In the reading of "أن" (anna) with a fatha there are two grammatical possibilities: one is the nominative (raf'), and the other is the accusative (nasb).

As for the nominative, it is on the basis of an implied prefix: the meaning is "that (is) so, [so] taste it, for indeed the disbelievers have the punishment of the Fire."

As for the accusative, it has two aspects. The first: it is governed by an implied verb, meaning "[ذلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ] and know and be certain that [أَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ]." The second: it means "and [for] the disbelievers" – and because the preposition (yā' of the genitive, i.e., the prepositional letter) was dropped, it is put in the accusative.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 5–14 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. The commentators differ over what the particle "ka" (as) in His words ﴿ka-ma﴾ is connected to. It may be a comparison (the kaf being for comparison; see al-Qurtubi's tafsir: 7/368) with God's bringing out His Prophet from his house in truth. ʿIkrima said: the meaning is ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾, for that is better for you, just as God's bringing Muhammad out of his house in truth was good for you, even though a group of you disliked it.

Mujahid said: ﴿As your Lord brought you out, O Muhammad, from your house in truth﴾, despite the dislike of a group of the believers, so they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it; that is, they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it as they did at Badr.

Some said: God commanded His Messenger, peace be upon him, to proceed with his command regarding the spoils despite the dislike of some of his companions, just as he proceeded with his command when he set out from his house to pursue the caravan while they were unwilling.

It was said: its meaning is ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ with disputation, just as they disputed with you on the day of Badr when they said: You brought us out for the caravan and did not inform us of fighting [so we would be displeased].

It was said: its meaning is ﴿Those are the true believers﴾ ﴿as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾.

Some said: the kaf means "upon"; its implied sense is: proceed upon that to which your Lord brought you out.

Ibn Hayyan said, from al-Kalbi: Abu ʿUbayda said it means an oath, its sense being: By Him who brought you out of your house in truth. It was also said: the kaf means "when," its implied sense being: When your Lord brought you out of your house in Medina to Badr in truth. [See Ibn al-Jawzi's Zad al-Masir: 3/218.]

﴿Indeed, a group of the believers were averse﴾ to the pursuit of the polytheists. ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth﴾, that is, concerning the fighting. This was because when the believers became certain of the armed strength and of war on the day of Badr, and understood that it was fighting, they disliked it and said: O Messenger of God, you did not inform us that we would meet the enemy so that we might prepare for battle; we only went out for the caravan. This is their dispute, ﴿after it had become clear to them﴾ that you do nothing except what God has commanded.

Ibn Zayd said: these are the polytheists who dispute with him concerning the truth, ﴿as if they were being driven to death﴾, meaning those who are called to Islam, because of their aversion to it, ﴿while they look on﴾.

﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾. The verse.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Yasar and al-Suddi said: Kurz ibn Jabir al-Qurashi raided the pasture of Medina until he reached al-Safra. The Prophet ﷺ was informed, so he rode in pursuit, but Kurz outpaced him, and the Prophet ﷺ returned and remained for a year. Abu Sufyan had come from Syria with a caravan of Quraysh in which were ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿAmr ibn Hisham, and Makhrama ibn Nawfal al-Zuhri, with forty riders from the nobles of Quraysh, and in it was great merchandise, namely the luggage caravan. When he was near Badr, the Prophet ﷺ received word, so he summoned his companions against them and informed them of the abundance of wealth and the scarcity of troops, saying: "This is the caravan of Quraysh, in which is their property; go out to it, perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will grant it to you as spoil." [216] They set out, intending only Abu Sufyan, and the riders did not regard it except as a spoil for themselves; some hastened and some were reluctant.

This was because they had not supposed that the Messenger of God ﷺ would meet battle. When Abu Sufyan heard of the Prophet's ﷺ march, he hired Damdam ibn ʿAmr al-Ghifari and sent him to Mecca, ordering him to come to Quraysh, call them to arms, and inform them that Muhammad had intercepted their caravan with his companions.

Damdam set out quickly for Mecca, and Satan went out with him in the form of Suraqa ibn Khatham. He came to Mecca and said: "Muhammad and his companions have intercepted your caravan. ﴿There is no one who can overcome you today among the people, and I am your protector﴾." The people of Mecca grew angry and rallied, calling out: "None of us shall stay behind; whoever does, we will demolish his house and plunder him." The Messenger of God ﷺ went out with his companions until he reached a valley called Wafran, and news reached him of Quraysh's march to protect their caravan. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, set out until, when they were at al-Ruha, he took a spy from the people, who informed him of them. The Messenger of God ﷺ also sent a spy of his own from Juhayna, an ally of the Ansar, named Ibn al-Uraiqit, who brought him news of the people. The caravan outran the Messenger of God ﷺ, and Gabriel descended and said: "God has promised you ﴿one of the two groups﴾, either the caravan or Quraysh." They preferred the caravan. The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions about pursuing the caravan or fighting the army. Abu Bakr stood and spoke well; ʿUmar stood and spoke well. Then al-Miqdad ibn ʿAmr stood and said: "O Messenger of God, proceed as God has commanded you, and we are with you. By God, we will not say as the children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 24]; rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight, and we are fighting with you. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us to Bark al-ʿImad, we would fight alongside you until we reached it."

The Messenger of God ﷺ said good things to him and prayed good for him. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Advise me, O people." [217]

He meant the Ansar, for when they pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqaba they had said: "O Messenger of God, we are free of your covenant until you reach our homes; when you reach our dwellings, you are under our protection, and we will defend you as we defend our sons and women." The Messenger of God ﷺ feared that the Ansar would not consider it incumbent upon them to support him except against one who attacked him in Medina, and that it was not incumbent upon them to send him to their enemy beyond their lands. When the Messenger of God ﷺ said that, Saʿd ibn Muʿadh said to him: "By God, it seems you mean us, O Messenger of God?"

He ﷺ said: "Indeed."

He said: "We have believed in you and confirmed you, and we testify that what you have brought is the truth, and we have given you our pledges and covenants of hearing and obedience. So proceed, O Messenger of God, with what you desire. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge in with you; not one man of us would stay behind. We do not dislike that our enemy should meet us with us tomorrow; we are steadfast in war and truthful at the encounter. Perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will show you from us what will delight your eye. So march with us in God's blessing."

The Prophet ﷺ was delighted by that, and Saʿd's words invigorated him. Then he said: "Proceed in God's blessing and rejoice, for God has promised you one of the two groups. By God, I am now looking at the places where the people will fall." [Fully, dispersed, in al-Tabari's tafsir: 9/145, 248, and Bayhaqi's Dala'il: 3/110.]

That is His words: ﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾, that is, of the two parties: one was Abu Sufyan with the caravan, and the other was Abu Jahl with the army. ﴿And you wished that the unarmed one would be yours﴾, meaning the caravan in which there was no fighting. ﴿Shawka﴾ is strength and power, and its root is from thorn (shawk). ﴿But God wills to establish the truth﴾, that is, to confirm it and make it manifest, ﴿by His words﴾, by His command to you to fight the unbelievers, ﴿and to cut off the last of the disbelievers﴾, so that He may uproot them, ﴿that He might establish the truth﴾, Islam, ﴿and nullify falsehood﴾, disbelief.

It was said: the truth is the Qur'an and falsehood is Satan. ﴿Though the guilty disliked it﴾, that is, the polytheists.

﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾, that is, sought refuge in Him from your enemy and asked Him for victory over them.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: On the day of Badr, when the Messenger of God ﷺ saw the multitude of polytheists and the scarcity of Muslims, he entered the tent, he and Abu Bakr, faced the qibla, and began to supplicate, saying: "O God, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O God, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on earth." He continued thus until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr took his cloak, placed it on his shoulders, embraced him from behind, and said: "O Prophet of God, enough of your entreating your Lord, for God will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you."

﴿So He answered you: "I will reinforce you﴾, that is, that I. ʿIsa read it with a kasra on the alif, "innī," and said: "Indeed I am reinforcing you and adding to you and sending aid to you ﴿with a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾." The people of Medina read ﴿murdifīn﴾ with a fatha on the dal, and the rest with a kasra; both are dialects meaning successive, following one another. It is said: "ardafahu" and "radafahu" both mean "to follow him." The poet said:

"When the Jawza' follows the Thurayya, I suspect the family of Fatima of suspicions" [Taj al-ʿArus: 6/115; Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/245].

He meant: "radafat" — came after it, because the Jawza' rises after the Thurayya. Whoever reads with a fatha, it is in the passive sense, meaning God reinforced the Muslims and brought it to them, and God reinforced them with angels. Gabriel descended with five hundred angels on the right wing, among whom was Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him; Michael descended with five hundred on the left, among whom was ʿAli, may God ennoble his face. They were in the form of men, wearing white garments and white turbans, their ends hanging between their shoulders. The angels fought on the day of Badr; they did not fight on the day of the Confederates, nor on the day of Hunayn, and they never fight except as reinforcements or as aid.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: While a man from the Muslims was running after a man from the polytheists, he heard a lash strike above him and the voice of a horseman saying: "Advance, Hayzum!" He looked at the polytheist ahead of him, who fell on his back; he looked at him, and his face was split and cut like the stroke of a whip. The man came and related this to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "You have spoken truly; that is from the reinforcement of heaven." That day they killed seventy and captured seventy. [218]

Mujahid said: The Prophet ﷺ was not reinforced, as God mentioned, except by the thousand of the angels ﴿following one another﴾ mentioned in al-Anfal; as for three thousand and five thousand, they were glad tidings.

﴿And God did not make it except as good news﴾, meaning the reinforcement.

al-Farra': meaning the reinforcements.

﴿And that your hearts might be reassured thereby. Victory is only from God. Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿When He covered you with drowsiness as security from Him﴾. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿yaghshikum﴾ with a fatha on the ya, with ﴿al-nuʿas﴾ in the nominative, taking the verb as having it as its subject, citing His words in Surat Al ʿImran: ﴿security, drowsiness overcoming a group of you﴾ [Surat Al ʿImran: 154], making the verb belong to it.

The people of Medina read ﴿yughshikum﴾ with a damma on the ya and lightened, taking the verb as God's, so that it would agree with His words ﴿and He sends down﴾ and ﴿and to purify you﴾; they cited His words, "as if their faces had been covered" [Surat Yunus: 27].

ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', ʿIkrima, al-Jahdari, ʿIsa, and the people of Kufa read ﴿yughashshikum﴾ with a damma on the ya and a shadda.

Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, citing His words ﴿and it covered what it covered﴾ [Surat al-Najm: 54]. "Al-nuʿas" is sleep, lightened. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the beginning of the people's... ﴿amanatan﴾ with a fatha on the mim is the reading of the common people; Abu Hayat and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿amnatan﴾ with a sukun on the mim, which is the verbal noun of your saying "amintu min kadha, amanan, amanatan, wa amanatan," all meaning the same, which is why it is in the accusative.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud said: Drowsiness in battle is security from God, mighty and majestic, and in prayer it is from Satan.

﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky﴾. This was because the Muslims had alighted at a green sand dune at Badr, into which the foot and the hooves of animals sink, while the polytheists had preceded them to the water of Badr al-ʿUzma and had taken control of it. In the morning some of the Muslims were in a state of minor impurity and some of major impurity; thirst afflicted them, and Satan whispered to them: "You claim that the Prophet of God is among you and that you are the friends of God, yet the polytheists have overcome you at the water, and you pray in impurity, minor and major. How, then, do you hope to triumph over them?"

He said: God, mighty and majestic, sent rain, from which the valley flowed; the believers drank from it, bathed, performed ablution, watered the mounts, and filled the water-skins. The dust settled, the ground was packed so that feet were firmly planted, the whisperings of Satan ceased, and their souls were content. This is His words: ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby﴾, from minor and major impurity.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read ﴿liyutahhirakum﴾ with a quiet ta' from "atharahu Allah," [purify].

﴿And to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾, that is, the whisper of Satan.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿rujzu﴾ with a damma on the ra'. Abu al-ʿAliya read ﴿rijs﴾ with a sin, as the Arabs interchange sin and zay, saying "bazaq" and "basaq."

"Al-sirat" and "al-zirat," "al-asad" and "al-azd."

﴿And to bind your hearts﴾ with certainty and patience, ﴿and to make firm the feet﴾, so that they do not slip in the sand, by packing the ground.

It was said: by patience and strength of heart.

﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you, so make firm those who believe"﴾, that is, with help and victory; so make firm those who believe, that is, illuminate their hearts, correct their resolve and their steadfastness in jihad. It was said: that making firm was by their presence with them in the battle.

It was said: their aid to them against their enemy. Abu Rawq said: the angel would appear in the form of a man whom they recognized; he would come to one of the Prophet's companions and say: "I have drawn near the polytheists and heard them say, 'By God, if they charge against us, we will surely [break them]'." The Muslims would then relate this to one another, which strengthened their souls and increased their boldness.

Ibn Ishaq and al-Mubarrad said: ﴿So make firm those who believe﴾, that is, support them. ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾. Then He taught them how to strike and kill, saying: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾.

Some said: this command is connected to His words, "so make firm those who believe."

Others said: it is a command from God, mighty and majestic, to the believers. They differed over His words ﴿above the necks﴾. ʿAtiyya and al-Dahhak said: it means strike the necks, as in His words ﴿when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾ [Surat Muhammad: 4].

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I was not sent to punish with the punishment of God, but I was sent to strike necks and to tighten bonds." [219]

Some said: it means "strike upon the necks," with "fawq" meaning "upon." ʿIkrima said: it means strike the heads above the necks. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means strike above the necks, that is, upon the necks; its parallel is His words ﴿if they are women above two﴾ [Surat al-Nisa': 11], meaning two or more than two.

﴿And strike from them every fingertip﴾. ʿAtiyya said: that is, every joint.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak said: it means the extremities; "banan" is the plural of "bananah," which are the tips of the fingers of the hands and feet, and its derivation is from "abana bi'l-maqam" when one stays in a place.

The poet said:

"Would that I had cut off his fingertip, and met him in the house, awake and wary" [The line is by ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas, as in Lisan al-ʿArab: 13/59].

Yaman ibn Ra'ab said: ﴿strike above the necks﴾ means the chieftains, and ﴿strike from them every fingertip﴾ means the lowly. The correct view is the first. Abu Dawud al-Mazini, who had witnessed Badr, said: I pursued a man from the polytheists to strike him on the day of Badr; his head fell before my sword reached him, so I knew that someone else had killed him.

Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf narrated from his father, who said: I saw on the day of Badr that one of us would point his sword at a polytheist, and his head would fall from his body before the sword reached him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: a man from the tribe of Ghifar told me: My cousin and I came and climbed a mountain to overlook Badr, and we were polytheists awaiting the outcome, to see on whom the defeat would fall, so we could plunder with the plunderers.

He said: While we were on the mountain, a cloud drew near us, and we heard in it the neighing of horses, and I heard a speaker say: "Advance, Hayzum!" [Hayzum was the name of Gabriel's horse.] As for my cousin, the veil over his heart was lifted and he died; as for me, I nearly perished, then I steadied myself.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 5–14 (part 2 of 2):

Ikrimah said: Abu Rafi', the freedman of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), said: "I was a slave of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and Islam had entered our household: Umm al-Fadl had embraced Islam, and I had embraced it too. But al-Abbas used to fear his people and disliked opposing them, so he concealed his Islam. He was a man of great wealth, dispersed among his people. Abu Lahab, the enemy of God, had stayed behind from Badr, and he sent in his place al-As ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughirah. They did this: no man stayed behind without sending another man in his place. When the news came of what had befallen the companions of Badr from Quraysh, God humiliated and disgraced him (Abu Lahab), and we felt in ourselves strength and resolve, though he (Abu Lahab) was a weak man." He said: "I used to make arrows, shaping them in the chamber of Zamzam. By God, I was sitting there shaping arrows, and with me sat Umm al-Fadl, and the news that had come had gladdened us, when the wicked Abu Lahab came dragging his feet until he sat at the edge of the chamber, with his back to my back. While he was sitting, people said: 'This is Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who has arrived.' Abu Lahab said: 'Come to me, nephew, tell me how the affair of the people went.' He said: 'Nothing, by God. It was as if, when we met them, we gave them the backs of their necks: they were killed and captured as they pleased. And by God, despite that, I did not blame the people:
We met men, white, on horses [suspended] between heaven and earth, [nothing could withstand them], and nothing could stand against them.'"
Abu Rafi' said: "I lifted the side of the chamber with my hand and then said: 'Those are the angels.' Abu Lahab raised his hand and struck my face a severe blow. I wrestled with him, and he threw me down and struck the ground with me, then he sat on me and beat me. I was a weak man. Umm al-Fadl got up, took one of the pillars of the house, and struck him a blow that split his head, a grievous wound. She said: 'Do you take advantage of him because his master is absent?' He got up and left, humiliated. By God, he did not live more than seven nights before God struck him with the 'adasah [[al-'adasah: a pustule resembling a lentil that appears on the body, of the kind of plague, which usually kills.]], and he died."
His sons left him for two or three nights without burying him, until he stank in his house. Quraysh used to avoid the 'adasah as people avoid plague. A man of Quraysh said to them: "Woe to you both! Are you not ashamed that your father has rotted in his house, and you do not wash him?" They said: "We fear this sore." He said: "Go, and we will go with you." So they did not wash him except by pouring water on him from afar, without touching him. Then they carried him and buried him at the upper part of Mecca, against a wall, and they threw stones upon him until they covered him [[Mustadrak al-Sahihayn: 3/322; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 6/89.]]."

It is narrated by Muqassam from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The one who took al-Abbas captive was Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr, brother of the Banu Salamah. Abu al-Yusr was a small, slight man, and al-Abbas was a large, heavy man. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abu al-Yusr: 'O Abu al-Yusr, how did you capture al-Abbas?'

He said: 'O Messenger of God, a man helped me against him whom I had not seen before or after, of such and such appearance.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'A noble angel helped you against him'" [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 4/103.]].

﴿ذلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ شاقُّوا اللَّهَ﴾ [That is because they opposed God]: they opposed God and His Messenger. ﴿وَمَنْ يُشاقِقِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ الْعِقابِ﴾ [And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment], meaning this is the punishment which He has hastened for you, O disbelievers. ﴿فَذُوقُوهُ﴾ [So taste it] now, ﴿وَأَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ [and that for the disbelievers] in the Hereafter ﴿عَذابَ النَّارِ﴾ [is the punishment of the Fire]. In the reading of "أن" (anna) with a fatha there are two grammatical possibilities: one is the nominative (raf'), and the other is the accusative (nasb).

As for the nominative, it is on the basis of an implied prefix: the meaning is "that (is) so, [so] taste it, for indeed the disbelievers have the punishment of the Fire."

As for the accusative, it has two aspects. The first: it is governed by an implied verb, meaning "[ذلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ] and know and be certain that [أَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ]." The second: it means "and [for] the disbelievers" – and because the preposition (yā' of the genitive, i.e., the prepositional letter) was dropped, it is put in the accusative.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 5–14 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. The commentators differ over what the particle "ka" (as) in His words ﴿ka-ma﴾ is connected to. It may be a comparison (the kaf being for comparison; see al-Qurtubi's tafsir: 7/368) with God's bringing out His Prophet from his house in truth. ʿIkrima said: the meaning is ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾, for that is better for you, just as God's bringing Muhammad out of his house in truth was good for you, even though a group of you disliked it.

Mujahid said: ﴿As your Lord brought you out, O Muhammad, from your house in truth﴾, despite the dislike of a group of the believers, so they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it; that is, they dislike fighting and dispute with you about it as they did at Badr.

Some said: God commanded His Messenger, peace be upon him, to proceed with his command regarding the spoils despite the dislike of some of his companions, just as he proceeded with his command when he set out from his house to pursue the caravan while they were unwilling.

It was said: its meaning is ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ with disputation, just as they disputed with you on the day of Badr when they said: You brought us out for the caravan and did not inform us of fighting [so we would be displeased].

It was said: its meaning is ﴿Those are the true believers﴾ ﴿as your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾.

Some said: the kaf means "upon"; its implied sense is: proceed upon that to which your Lord brought you out.

Ibn Hayyan said, from al-Kalbi: Abu ʿUbayda said it means an oath, its sense being: By Him who brought you out of your house in truth. It was also said: the kaf means "when," its implied sense being: When your Lord brought you out of your house in Medina to Badr in truth. [See Ibn al-Jawzi's Zad al-Masir: 3/218.]

﴿Indeed, a group of the believers were averse﴾ to the pursuit of the polytheists. ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth﴾, that is, concerning the fighting. This was because when the believers became certain of the armed strength and of war on the day of Badr, and understood that it was fighting, they disliked it and said: O Messenger of God, you did not inform us that we would meet the enemy so that we might prepare for battle; we only went out for the caravan. This is their dispute, ﴿after it had become clear to them﴾ that you do nothing except what God has commanded.

Ibn Zayd said: these are the polytheists who dispute with him concerning the truth, ﴿as if they were being driven to death﴾, meaning those who are called to Islam, because of their aversion to it, ﴿while they look on﴾.

﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾. The verse.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Yasar and al-Suddi said: Kurz ibn Jabir al-Qurashi raided the pasture of Medina until he reached al-Safra. The Prophet ﷺ was informed, so he rode in pursuit, but Kurz outpaced him, and the Prophet ﷺ returned and remained for a year. Abu Sufyan had come from Syria with a caravan of Quraysh in which were ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, ʿAmr ibn Hisham, and Makhrama ibn Nawfal al-Zuhri, with forty riders from the nobles of Quraysh, and in it was great merchandise, namely the luggage caravan. When he was near Badr, the Prophet ﷺ received word, so he summoned his companions against them and informed them of the abundance of wealth and the scarcity of troops, saying: "This is the caravan of Quraysh, in which is their property; go out to it, perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will grant it to you as spoil." [216] They set out, intending only Abu Sufyan, and the riders did not regard it except as a spoil for themselves; some hastened and some were reluctant.

This was because they had not supposed that the Messenger of God ﷺ would meet battle. When Abu Sufyan heard of the Prophet's ﷺ march, he hired Damdam ibn ʿAmr al-Ghifari and sent him to Mecca, ordering him to come to Quraysh, call them to arms, and inform them that Muhammad had intercepted their caravan with his companions.

Damdam set out quickly for Mecca, and Satan went out with him in the form of Suraqa ibn Khatham. He came to Mecca and said: "Muhammad and his companions have intercepted your caravan. ﴿There is no one who can overcome you today among the people, and I am your protector﴾." The people of Mecca grew angry and rallied, calling out: "None of us shall stay behind; whoever does, we will demolish his house and plunder him." The Messenger of God ﷺ went out with his companions until he reached a valley called Wafran, and news reached him of Quraysh's march to protect their caravan. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, set out until, when they were at al-Ruha, he took a spy from the people, who informed him of them. The Messenger of God ﷺ also sent a spy of his own from Juhayna, an ally of the Ansar, named Ibn al-Uraiqit, who brought him news of the people. The caravan outran the Messenger of God ﷺ, and Gabriel descended and said: "God has promised you ﴿one of the two groups﴾, either the caravan or Quraysh." They preferred the caravan. The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions about pursuing the caravan or fighting the army. Abu Bakr stood and spoke well; ʿUmar stood and spoke well. Then al-Miqdad ibn ʿAmr stood and said: "O Messenger of God, proceed as God has commanded you, and we are with you. By God, we will not say as the children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 24]; rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight, and we are fighting with you. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us to Bark al-ʿImad, we would fight alongside you until we reached it."

The Messenger of God ﷺ said good things to him and prayed good for him. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Advise me, O people." [217]

He meant the Ansar, for when they pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqaba they had said: "O Messenger of God, we are free of your covenant until you reach our homes; when you reach our dwellings, you are under our protection, and we will defend you as we defend our sons and women." The Messenger of God ﷺ feared that the Ansar would not consider it incumbent upon them to support him except against one who attacked him in Medina, and that it was not incumbent upon them to send him to their enemy beyond their lands. When the Messenger of God ﷺ said that, Saʿd ibn Muʿadh said to him: "By God, it seems you mean us, O Messenger of God?"

He ﷺ said: "Indeed."

He said: "We have believed in you and confirmed you, and we testify that what you have brought is the truth, and we have given you our pledges and covenants of hearing and obedience. So proceed, O Messenger of God, with what you desire. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge in with you; not one man of us would stay behind. We do not dislike that our enemy should meet us with us tomorrow; we are steadfast in war and truthful at the encounter. Perhaps God, mighty and majestic, will show you from us what will delight your eye. So march with us in God's blessing."

The Prophet ﷺ was delighted by that, and Saʿd's words invigorated him. Then he said: "Proceed in God's blessing and rejoice, for God has promised you one of the two groups. By God, I am now looking at the places where the people will fall." [Fully, dispersed, in al-Tabari's tafsir: 9/145, 248, and Bayhaqi's Dala'il: 3/110.]
