We met men, white, on horses [suspended] between heaven and earth, [nothing could withstand them], and nothing could stand against them.'"
Abu Rafi' said: "I lifted the side of the chamber with my hand and then said: 'Those are the angels.' Abu Lahab raised his hand and struck my face a severe blow. I wrestled with him, and he threw me down and struck the ground with me, then he sat on me and beat me. I was a weak man. Umm al-Fadl got up, took one of the pillars of the house, and struck him a blow that split his head, a grievous wound. She said: 'Do you take advantage of him because his master is absent?' He got up and left, humiliated. By God, he did not live more than seven nights before God struck him with the 'adasah [[al-'adasah: a pustule resembling a lentil that appears on the body, of the kind of plague, which usually kills.]], and he died."
His sons left him for two or three nights without burying him, until he stank in his house. Quraysh used to avoid the 'adasah as people avoid plague. A man of Quraysh said to them: "Woe to you both! Are you not ashamed that your father has rotted in his house, and you do not wash him?" They said: "We fear this sore." He said: "Go, and we will go with you." So they did not wash him except by pouring water on him from afar, without touching him. Then they carried him and buried him at the upper part of Mecca, against a wall, and they threw stones upon him until they covered him [[Mustadrak al-Sahihayn: 3/322; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 6/89.]]."

It is narrated by Muqassam from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The one who took al-Abbas captive was Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr, brother of the Banu Salamah. Abu al-Yusr was a small, slight man, and al-Abbas was a large, heavy man. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Abu al-Yusr: 'O Abu al-Yusr, how did you capture al-Abbas?'

He said: 'O Messenger of God, a man helped me against him whom I had not seen before or after, of such and such appearance.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'A noble angel helped you against him'" [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 4/103.]].

﴿ذلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ شاقُّوا اللَّهَ﴾ [That is because they opposed God]: they opposed God and His Messenger. ﴿وَمَنْ يُشاقِقِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ الْعِقابِ﴾ [And whoever opposes God and His Messenger, indeed God is severe in punishment], meaning this is the punishment which He has hastened for you, O disbelievers. ﴿فَذُوقُوهُ﴾ [So taste it] now, ﴿وَأَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ [and that for the disbelievers] in the Hereafter ﴿عَذابَ النَّارِ﴾ [is the punishment of the Fire]. In the reading of "أن" (anna) with a fatha there are two grammatical possibilities: one is the nominative (raf'), and the other is the accusative (nasb).

As for the nominative, it is on the basis of an implied prefix: the meaning is "that (is) so, [so] taste it, for indeed the disbelievers have the punishment of the Fire."

As for the accusative, it has two aspects. The first: it is governed by an implied verb, meaning "[ذلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ] and know and be certain that [أَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ]." The second: it means "and [for] the disbelievers" – and because the preposition (yā' of the genitive, i.e., the prepositional letter) was dropped, it is put in the accusative.

O you who believe! When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle), do not turn your backs to them. (﴿إِذَا لَقِيتُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا زَحْفًا فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾)

*Zahfan* means: [defeated] drawing close to one another, (i.e.) some of you approaching others. *Al-tazahhuf* (the drawing near and converging of two armies) means drawing close and coming near.

Al-A'sha said:

"For whom are the enmities? Their march is a rumbling, like a great ship that is tossed about when the tossing begins."

*Al-zahf* is a verbal noun (masdar), which is why it is not pluralised, as in their saying: "a just people" (qawm 'adl) and "a satisfied people" (qawm ridan).

﴿فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾ means: do not turn your backs to them so that you flee from them, but stand firm against them.

﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾: [whoever turns his back to them on that day], i.e. his back. Al-Hasan read *dubura* with a sukun (dubur).

﴿إِلَّا مُتَحَرِّفًا لِقِتَالٍ﴾: i.e. one who swerves (*mutaʿattifan*) or withdraws (*mustaṭriden*) for battle, by seeking an opening in his enemy that will enable him to strike him, and so he turns back upon him. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/265.]

﴿أَوْ مُتَحَيِّزًا﴾: i.e. one who joins (*munḍammun*) and remains steadfast, ﴿إِلَى فِئَةٍ﴾: a group of believers who will rally to him so that he may return to the fight. ﴿فَقَدْ بَاءَ بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمَأْوَاهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the ruling of His saying ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse): whether it is specific to the people of Badr or applies to all believers.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: This applied only on the day of Badr. They were not permitted to withdraw, even to join the polytheists. On that day there was no Muslim on earth other than them, and the Muslims had no one [to rally to] except the Prophet (ﷺ). But after that, the Muslims are a group [who rally] to one another, [as in] the one "composed" (of a unified force). This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatada.

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: God made the Fire obligatory for whoever fled on the day of Badr, and He said: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse). Then, when the day of Uhud came after that, He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا اسْتَزَلَّهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا كَسَبُوا وَلَقَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 155]. Then the day of Hunayn came seven years later, and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ﴾ ... ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 25–27].

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: This verse was abrogated (*mansukha*, see *naskh* – abrogation) by His saying: ﴿الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 66] and what follows. So it is not permitted for a people to flee from twice their number. That verse was abrogated, except for this numerical limit.

Al-Kalbi said: Whoever faces the day, advancing or retreating, is a martyr, but the one who advances has preceded the one who retreats into Paradise.

Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: A man fled from (the battle of) al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I have fled from the battle." 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: "I am your group (*fi'ah*)."

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: When Abu 'Ubayd was killed, news reached 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a group for him [so I am a group for every Muslim]."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: We were at Masil, [where] the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent us out. The people charged into a rout, and we fled. We said: "We will flee into the land out of shame at what we have done," and we entered the houses.

Then we said: "O Messenger of God, we are the fleeing ones." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the ones who return to the attack, and we are the group of the Muslims."

[220] [Bada'i' al-Sana'i': 7/99; al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya: 4/283.]

Others said: Rather, our ruling is general, applying to everyone who turns his back on the enemy. Among them is one who narrated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to some of his family: "Beware of fleeing from the battle, for if they perish, then stand firm, for [...]" except in the case of committing major sins, and except for polytheism with God, and fleeing from the battle, because God Most High says: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse).

﴿فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ﴾ (the verse).

The people of tafsir and of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived at Badr, he said: "These are the places where the people will fall, God willing." When they [the polytheists] came into view, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is Quraysh; they have come with their arrogance and pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Gabriel came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them."

When the two hosts met, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley." He handed him pebbles mixed with dust, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw them into the faces of the people and said: "May the faces be disfigured (*shāhat al-wujūh*)."

No polytheist remained who did not get some of it in his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils. Then the believers pursued them, killing and capturing them, and that throw was the cause of the rout. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/270–271.]

Hakim ibn Hizam said: On the day of Badr we heard a sound fall from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw that throw, and we fled.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took three pebbles on the day of Badr: he threw one pebble at the right wing of the enemy, one at their left wing, and one in the midst of them, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and they fled. [222] [Ibid.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it, and said: "O Muhammad, will God give life to this when it is decayed?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will cause you to enter the Fire." When the day of Badr came, he [Ubayy] was taken prisoner, then he was ransomed. When he had been ransomed, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have a horse that I feed a *faraq* of grain every day, so that I may kill you upon it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing."

When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf came charging on that horse until he drew close to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Step back (*istākhirū*)!" They stepped back. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up with a spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The spear broke and struck one of his ribs, and Ubayy returned to his companions, heavy [with the wound]. They carried him and began saying: "There is no harm." But Ubayy said: "By God, if it had been spread among the people, it would have killed them all! Did he not say, 'I will kill you, God willing'?" His companions took him away mourning him, until he died at a place along the road. They buried him, and concerning that God revealed this verse: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ (the verse). [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/46.]

Safwan ibn 'Amr narrated from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn [Jubayr] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Khaybar asked for a bow. A long bow was brought to him, and he said: "Bring me something else." They brought him a stiff bow (*qaws kabdā'*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) shot at the fortress. The arrow came down until it killed Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. Then God Most High revealed: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ﴾. This is the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) of the verse. [Asbab al-Nuzul: 156; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/308.]

As for its meaning: God Most High attributed the killing and the throwing to Himself, because from Him, Most High, came the causing and the making accurate (*al-tasbib wa al-tasdid*), and from His Messenger and the believers came the striking and the casting. Likewise all other human acts are acquired from God, who originates and brings them into being through eternal, perfect power, while from creatures comes the acquisition (*al-iktisab*) through created faculties. In this statement there is evidence for the establishment of the doctrine of the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) and the falsity of the view of the Qadariyya.

It was said: He attributed it to Himself only so that the people would not be vain (*li-allā yuʿjaba al-qawm*).

Mujahid said: [The companions] said: "I killed," and another said: "I killed," so God revealed this verse.

Al-Hasan said: He meant: "You did not cause them to die, but God caused them to die, and you wounded them, because the release of the soul is to Him, not to anyone else."

He said: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾, i.e. [killed], reaching the polytheists with it and filling their eyes with it.

Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: that throw was not yours were it not for what God placed in it of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy because of it, until He routed them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning "He gave you victory." Al-A'mash said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: He granted you success and made your throw accurate.

[Author's note: What I have stated is derived from the verse itself; the verse intends to place the strike of the Greatest Messenger in the position of the strike of the Exalted Creator. So although the Messenger is the thrower, God Most High is the thrower, and it is in the force of the famous sacred hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts [and acts of worship] until I love him; when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks." See Ghawali al-La'ali: 4/103 no. 152; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/229 no. 1155.]

﴿وَلِيُبْلِيَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْهُ بَلَاءً حَسَنًا﴾: i.e. and that He might bestow upon the believers a great favour through victory, spoils, reward and recompense.

Ibn Ishaq said: [That He might make the believers know the blessing of their victory and their triumph over their enemy despite their small number and their enemy's great number, so that they would know His right and thank Him for His blessings]. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ﴾ of their words, ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ of their deeds; He hears their secrets and knows their inner thoughts.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾: i.e. what I have mentioned of killing, throwing and the good trial. ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e. and know that God [...]. Concerning the opening of *anna* (the reading with fatha), there are the aspects found in His saying: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ وَأَنَّ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَذَابَ النَّارِ﴾ [and we have explained it there].

﴿مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾: weakening (*mudʿif*) the plotting of the disbelievers. The people of Hijaz, Syria and Basra read *muwahhinun* with tashdid and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative. Most of the people of Kufa read *muhinun* with takhfif and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative, and this was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash and Hafs read *muhinu kaydi*, with light pronunciation and idafa in the genitive. Whoever reads with tanwin means: "weakens." Whoever reads with takhfif and idafa, the lightness is shortened, as in His saying: ﴿مُرْسِلُو النَّاقَةِ﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 27] and ﴿كَاشِفُو الْعَذَابِ﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 15]. *Wahana* and *awhana* are two sound and eloquent dialects.

﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾: This is because Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O God, whichever of us is the more wicked and the more severing of kinship, and has brought what we do not know, give us victory over him." God answered his supplication and brought victory, and the two sons of 'Afra', 'Awf and Mas'ud, struck him, and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud finished him off. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/274.]

Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: When the polytheists set out from Mecca towards the Prophet (ﷺ), they clung to the curtains of the Ka'ba and said: "O God, give us victory over the two parties, guide the two factions, honour the two armies, and favour the two religions." So God revealed this verse.

'Ikrima said: The polytheists said: "O God, we do not know what Muhammad has brought, so judge between us and him in truth." So God revealed: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek a judgement, the judgement has come to you.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: This is an address to the companions of the Messenger of God. God said to the Muslims: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek victory from God and ask Him for conquest, then ﴿فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. with the help.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We complained to the Messenger of God (ʿalayhi al-salām), saying: "Do not seek victory for us." His face reddened, and he said: "A man before you would be seized, a pit would be dug for him in the ground, then a saw would be brought and he would be cut in two; nothing would turn him from his religion. Iron combs would scrape his flesh and sinews down to the bone, and nothing would turn him from his religion. This matter will certainly be completed by God, until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt and fears nothing but God, and the wolf [fears nothing] for his sheep. But you are being hasty." [224] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/109; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 4/63.]

Then He said to the disbelievers: ﴿وَإِنْ تَنْتَهُوا﴾ from disbelief in God and fighting His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to fight him and wage war against him, ﴿نَعُدْ﴾ with the like of the event that befell you on the day of Badr. [Cf. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/387.]

It was said: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to this statement and to fighting Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿وَلَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْكُمْ فِئَتُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ كَثُرَتْ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The people of Medina and Syria [read] *wa-anna Allāha* with the *alif* opened, meaning: "and because God [...]." It was said: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

The rest read it with kasra, as a new sentence (*istiʾnaf*), and they differed concerning it. Abu Hatim's reading is "*li-anna*" (because), and in the reading of 'Abdullah: "and God is with the believers."

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَا تَوَلَّوْا عَنْهُ﴾: do not turn away from His Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ his command, his ally (*waliyyuhu*).

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ the Qur'an and its admonitions. ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا﴾: meaning the hypocrites and the polytheists who heard the Book of God with their ears and said "We have heard," ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning they do not take admonition from the Qur'an, nor benefit from their hearing, as if they had not heard the truth.

O you who believe! When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle), do not turn your backs to them. (﴿إِذَا لَقِيتُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا زَحْفًا فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾)

*Zahfan* means: [defeated] drawing close to one another, (i.e.) some of you approaching others. *Al-tazahhuf* (the drawing near and converging of two armies) means drawing close and coming near.

Al-A'sha said:

"For whom are the enmities? Their march is a rumbling, like a great ship that is tossed about when the tossing begins."

*Al-zahf* is a verbal noun (masdar), which is why it is not pluralised, as in their saying: "a just people" (qawm 'adl) and "a satisfied people" (qawm ridan).

﴿فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾ means: do not turn your backs to them so that you flee from them, but stand firm against them.

﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾: [whoever turns his back to them on that day], i.e. his back. Al-Hasan read *dubura* with a sukun (dubur).

﴿إِلَّا مُتَحَرِّفًا لِقِتَالٍ﴾: i.e. one who swerves (*mutaʿattifan*) or withdraws (*mustaṭriden*) for battle, by seeking an opening in his enemy that will enable him to strike him, and so he turns back upon him. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/265.]

﴿أَوْ مُتَحَيِّزًا﴾: i.e. one who joins (*munḍammun*) and remains steadfast, ﴿إِلَى فِئَةٍ﴾: a group of believers who will rally to him so that he may return to the fight. ﴿فَقَدْ بَاءَ بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمَأْوَاهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the ruling of His saying ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse): whether it is specific to the people of Badr or applies to all believers.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: This applied only on the day of Badr. They were not permitted to withdraw, even to join the polytheists. On that day there was no Muslim on earth other than them, and the Muslims had no one [to rally to] except the Prophet (ﷺ). But after that, the Muslims are a group [who rally] to one another, [as in] the one "composed" (of a unified force). This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatada.

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: God made the Fire obligatory for whoever fled on the day of Badr, and He said: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse). Then, when the day of Uhud came after that, He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا اسْتَزَلَّهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا كَسَبُوا وَلَقَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 155]. Then the day of Hunayn came seven years later, and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ﴾ ... ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 25–27].

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: This verse was abrogated (*mansukha*, see *naskh* – abrogation) by His saying: ﴿الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 66] and what follows. So it is not permitted for a people to flee from twice their number. That verse was abrogated, except for this numerical limit.

Al-Kalbi said: Whoever faces the day, advancing or retreating, is a martyr, but the one who advances has preceded the one who retreats into Paradise.

Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: A man fled from (the battle of) al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I have fled from the battle." 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: "I am your group (*fi'ah*)."

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: When Abu 'Ubayd was killed, news reached 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a group for him [so I am a group for every Muslim]."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: We were at Masil, [where] the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent us out. The people charged into a rout, and we fled. We said: "We will flee into the land out of shame at what we have done," and we entered the houses.

Then we said: "O Messenger of God, we are the fleeing ones." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the ones who return to the attack, and we are the group of the Muslims."

[220] [Bada'i' al-Sana'i': 7/99; al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya: 4/283.]

Others said: Rather, our ruling is general, applying to everyone who turns his back on the enemy. Among them is one who narrated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to some of his family: "Beware of fleeing from the battle, for if they perish, then stand firm, for [...]" except in the case of committing major sins, and except for polytheism with God, and fleeing from the battle, because God Most High says: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse).

﴿فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ﴾ (the verse).

The people of tafsir and of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived at Badr, he said: "These are the places where the people will fall, God willing." When they [the polytheists] came into view, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is Quraysh; they have come with their arrogance and pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Gabriel came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them."

When the two hosts met, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley." He handed him pebbles mixed with dust, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw them into the faces of the people and said: "May the faces be disfigured (*shāhat al-wujūh*)."

No polytheist remained who did not get some of it in his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils. Then the believers pursued them, killing and capturing them, and that throw was the cause of the rout. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/270–271.]

Hakim ibn Hizam said: On the day of Badr we heard a sound fall from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw that throw, and we fled.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took three pebbles on the day of Badr: he threw one pebble at the right wing of the enemy, one at their left wing, and one in the midst of them, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and they fled. [222] [Ibid.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it, and said: "O Muhammad, will God give life to this when it is decayed?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will cause you to enter the Fire." When the day of Badr came, he [Ubayy] was taken prisoner, then he was ransomed. When he had been ransomed, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have a horse that I feed a *faraq* of grain every day, so that I may kill you upon it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing."

When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf came charging on that horse until he drew close to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Step back (*istākhirū*)!" They stepped back. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up with a spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The spear broke and struck one of his ribs, and Ubayy returned to his companions, heavy [with the wound]. They carried him and began saying: "There is no harm." But Ubayy said: "By God, if it had been spread among the people, it would have killed them all! Did he not say, 'I will kill you, God willing'?" His companions took him away mourning him, until he died at a place along the road. They buried him, and concerning that God revealed this verse: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ (the verse). [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/46.]

Safwan ibn 'Amr narrated from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn [Jubayr] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Khaybar asked for a bow. A long bow was brought to him, and he said: "Bring me something else." They brought him a stiff bow (*qaws kabdā'*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) shot at the fortress. The arrow came down until it killed Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. Then God Most High revealed: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ﴾. This is the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) of the verse. [Asbab al-Nuzul: 156; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/308.]

As for its meaning: God Most High attributed the killing and the throwing to Himself, because from Him, Most High, came the causing and the making accurate (*al-tasbib wa al-tasdid*), and from His Messenger and the believers came the striking and the casting. Likewise all other human acts are acquired from God, who originates and brings them into being through eternal, perfect power, while from creatures comes the acquisition (*al-iktisab*) through created faculties. In this statement there is evidence for the establishment of the doctrine of the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) and the falsity of the view of the Qadariyya.

It was said: He attributed it to Himself only so that the people would not be vain (*li-allā yuʿjaba al-qawm*).

Mujahid said: [The companions] said: "I killed," and another said: "I killed," so God revealed this verse.

Al-Hasan said: He meant: "You did not cause them to die, but God caused them to die, and you wounded them, because the release of the soul is to Him, not to anyone else."

He said: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾, i.e. [killed], reaching the polytheists with it and filling their eyes with it.

Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: that throw was not yours were it not for what God placed in it of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy because of it, until He routed them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning "He gave you victory." Al-A'mash said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: He granted you success and made your throw accurate.

[224] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/109; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 4/63.]

Then He said to the disbelievers: ﴿وَإِنْ تَنْتَهُوا﴾ from disbelief in God and fighting His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to fight him and wage war against him, ﴿نَعُدْ﴾ with the like of the event that befell you on the day of Badr. [Cf. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/387.]

It was said: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to this statement and to fighting Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿وَلَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْكُمْ فِئَتُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ كَثُرَتْ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The people of Medina and Syria [read] *wa-anna Allāha* with the *alif* opened, meaning: "and because God [...]." It was said: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

The rest read it with kasra, as a new sentence (*istiʾnaf*), and they differed concerning it. Abu Hatim's reading is "*li-anna*" (because), and in the reading of 'Abdullah: "and God is with the believers."

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَا تَوَلَّوْا عَنْهُ﴾: do not turn away from His Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ his command, his ally (*waliyyuhu*).

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ the Qur'an and its admonitions. ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا﴾: meaning the hypocrites and the polytheists who heard the Book of God with their ears and said "We have heard," ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning they do not take admonition from the Qur'an, nor benefit from their hearing, as if they had not heard the truth.

O you who believe! When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle), do not turn your backs to them. (﴿إِذَا لَقِيتُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا زَحْفًا فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾)

*Zahfan* means: [defeated] drawing close to one another, (i.e.) some of you approaching others. *Al-tazahhuf* (the drawing near and converging of two armies) means drawing close and coming near.

Al-A'sha said:

"For whom are the enmities? Their march is a rumbling, like a great ship that is tossed about when the tossing begins."

*Al-zahf* is a verbal noun (masdar), which is why it is not pluralised, as in their saying: "a just people" (qawm 'adl) and "a satisfied people" (qawm ridan).

﴿فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾ means: do not turn your backs to them so that you flee from them, but stand firm against them.

﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾: [whoever turns his back to them on that day], i.e. his back. Al-Hasan read *dubura* with a sukun (dubur).

﴿إِلَّا مُتَحَرِّفًا لِقِتَالٍ﴾: i.e. one who swerves (*mutaʿattifan*) or withdraws (*mustaṭriden*) for battle, by seeking an opening in his enemy that will enable him to strike him, and so he turns back upon him. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/265.]

﴿أَوْ مُتَحَيِّزًا﴾: i.e. one who joins (*munḍammun*) and remains steadfast, ﴿إِلَى فِئَةٍ﴾: a group of believers who will rally to him so that he may return to the fight. ﴿فَقَدْ بَاءَ بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمَأْوَاهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the ruling of His saying ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse): whether it is specific to the people of Badr or applies to all believers.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: This applied only on the day of Badr. They were not permitted to withdraw, even to join the polytheists. On that day there was no Muslim on earth other than them, and the Muslims had no one [to rally to] except the Prophet (ﷺ). But after that, the Muslims are a group [who rally] to one another, [as in] the one "composed" (of a unified force). This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatada.

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: God made the Fire obligatory for whoever fled on the day of Badr, and He said: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse). Then, when the day of Uhud came after that, He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا اسْتَزَلَّهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا كَسَبُوا وَلَقَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 155]. Then the day of Hunayn came seven years later, and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ﴾ ... ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 25–27].

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: This verse was abrogated (*mansukha*, see *naskh* – abrogation) by His saying: ﴿الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 66] and what follows. So it is not permitted for a people to flee from twice their number. That verse was abrogated, except for this numerical limit.

Al-Kalbi said: Whoever faces the day, advancing or retreating, is a martyr, but the one who advances has preceded the one who retreats into Paradise.

Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: A man fled from (the battle of) al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I have fled from the battle." 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: "I am your group (*fi'ah*)."

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: When Abu 'Ubayd was killed, news reached 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a group for him [so I am a group for every Muslim]."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: We were at Masil, [where] the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent us out. The people charged into a rout, and we fled. We said: "We will flee into the land out of shame at what we have done," and we entered the houses.

Then we said: "O Messenger of God, we are the fleeing ones." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the ones who return to the attack, and we are the group of the Muslims."

[220] [Bada'i' al-Sana'i': 7/99; al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya: 4/283.]

Others said: Rather, our ruling is general, applying to everyone who turns his back on the enemy. Among them is one who narrated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to some of his family: "Beware of fleeing from the battle, for if they perish, then stand firm, for [...]" except in the case of committing major sins, and except for polytheism with God, and fleeing from the battle, because God Most High says: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse).

﴿فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ﴾ (the verse).

The people of tafsir and of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived at Badr, he said: "These are the places where the people will fall, God willing." When they [the polytheists] came into view, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is Quraysh; they have come with their arrogance and pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Gabriel came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them."

When the two hosts met, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley." He handed him pebbles mixed with dust, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw them into the faces of the people and said: "May the faces be disfigured (*shāhat al-wujūh*)."

No polytheist remained who did not get some of it in his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils. Then the believers pursued them, killing and capturing them, and that throw was the cause of the rout. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/270–271.]

Hakim ibn Hizam said: On the day of Badr we heard a sound fall from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw that throw, and we fled.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took three pebbles on the day of Badr: he threw one pebble at the right wing of the enemy, one at their left wing, and one in the midst of them, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and they fled. [222] [Ibid.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it, and said: "O Muhammad, will God give life to this when it is decayed?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will cause you to enter the Fire." When the day of Badr came, he [Ubayy] was taken prisoner, then he was ransomed. When he had been ransomed, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have a horse that I feed a *faraq* of grain every day, so that I may kill you upon it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing."

When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf came charging on that horse until he drew close to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Step back (*istākhirū*)!" They stepped back. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up with a spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The spear broke and struck one of his ribs, and Ubayy returned to his companions, heavy [with the wound]. They carried him and began saying: "There is no harm." But Ubayy said: "By God, if it had been spread among the people, it would have killed them all! Did he not say, 'I will kill you, God willing'?" His companions took him away mourning him, until he died at a place along the road. They buried him, and concerning that God revealed this verse: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ (the verse). [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/46.]

Safwan ibn 'Amr narrated from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn [Jubayr] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Khaybar asked for a bow. A long bow was brought to him, and he said: "Bring me something else." They brought him a stiff bow (*qaws kabdā'*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) shot at the fortress. The arrow came down until it killed Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. Then God Most High revealed: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ﴾. This is the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) of the verse. [Asbab al-Nuzul: 156; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/308.]

As for its meaning: God Most High attributed the killing and the throwing to Himself, because from Him, Most High, came the causing and the making accurate (*al-tasbib wa al-tasdid*), and from His Messenger and the believers came the striking and the casting. Likewise all other human acts are acquired from God, who originates and brings them into being through eternal, perfect power, while from creatures comes the acquisition (*al-iktisab*) through created faculties. In this statement there is evidence for the establishment of the doctrine of the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) and the falsity of the view of the Qadariyya.

It was said: He attributed it to Himself only so that the people would not be vain (*li-allā yuʿjaba al-qawm*).

Mujahid said: [The companions] said: "I killed," and another said: "I killed," so God revealed this verse.

Al-Hasan said: He meant: "You did not cause them to die, but God caused them to die, and you wounded them, because the release of the soul is to Him, not to anyone else."

He said: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾, i.e. [killed], reaching the polytheists with it and filling their eyes with it.

Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: that throw was not yours were it not for what God placed in it of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy because of it, until He routed them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning "He gave you victory." Al-A'mash said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: He granted you success and made your throw accurate.

[Author's note: What I have stated is derived from the verse itself; the verse intends to place the strike of the Greatest Messenger in the position of the strike of the Exalted Creator. So although the Messenger is the thrower, God Most High is the thrower, and it is in the force of the famous sacred hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts [and acts of worship] until I love him; when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks." See Ghawali al-La'ali: 4/103 no. 152; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/229 no. 1155.]

﴿وَلِيُبْلِيَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْهُ بَلَاءً حَسَنًا﴾: i.e. and that He might bestow upon the believers a great favour through victory, spoils, reward and recompense.

Ibn Ishaq said: [That He might make the believers know the blessing of their victory and their triumph over their enemy despite their small number and their enemy's great number, so that they would know His right and thank Him for His blessings]. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ﴾ of their words, ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ of their deeds; He hears their secrets and knows their inner thoughts.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾: i.e. what I have mentioned of killing, throwing and the good trial. ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e. and know that God [...]. Concerning the opening of *anna* (the reading with fatha), there are the aspects found in His saying: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ وَأَنَّ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَذَابَ النَّارِ﴾ [and we have explained it there].

﴿مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾: weakening (*mudʿif*) the plotting of the disbelievers. The people of Hijaz, Syria and Basra read *muwahhinun* with tashdid and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative. Most of the people of Kufa read *muhinun* with takhfif and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative, and this was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash and Hafs read *muhinu kaydi*, with light pronunciation and idafa in the genitive. Whoever reads with tanwin means: "weakens." Whoever reads with takhfif and idafa, the lightness is shortened, as in His saying: ﴿مُرْسِلُو النَّاقَةِ﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 27] and ﴿كَاشِفُو الْعَذَابِ﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 15]. *Wahana* and *awhana* are two sound and eloquent dialects.

﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾: This is because Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O God, whichever of us is the more wicked and the more severing of kinship, and has brought what we do not know, give us victory over him." God answered his supplication and brought victory, and the two sons of 'Afra', 'Awf and Mas'ud, struck him, and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud finished him off. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/274.]

Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: When the polytheists set out from Mecca towards the Prophet (ﷺ), they clung to the curtains of the Ka'ba and said: "O God, give us victory over the two parties, guide the two factions, honour the two armies, and favour the two religions." So God revealed this verse.

'Ikrima said: The polytheists said: "O God, we do not know what Muhammad has brought, so judge between us and him in truth." So God revealed: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek a judgement, the judgement has come to you.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: This is an address to the companions of the Messenger of God. God said to the Muslims: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek victory from God and ask Him for conquest, then ﴿فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. with the help.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We complained to the Messenger of God (ʿalayhi al-salām), saying: "Do not seek victory for us." His face reddened, and he said: "A man before you would be seized, a pit would be dug for him in the ground, then a saw would be brought and he would be cut in two; nothing would turn him from his religion. Iron combs would scrape his flesh and sinews down to the bone, and nothing would turn him from his religion. This matter will certainly be completed by God, until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt and fears nothing but God, and the wolf [fears nothing] for his sheep. But you are being hasty." [224] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/109; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 4/63.]

﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾: [whoever turns his back to them on that day], i.e. his back. Al-Hasan read *dubura* with a sukun (dubur).
