Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: God made the Fire obligatory for whoever fled on the day of Badr, and He said: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse). Then, when the day of Uhud came after that, He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا اسْتَزَلَّهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا كَسَبُوا وَلَقَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 155]. Then the day of Hunayn came seven years later, and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ﴾ ... ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 25–27].

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: This verse was abrogated (*mansukha*, see *naskh* – abrogation) by His saying: ﴿الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 66] and what follows. So it is not permitted for a people to flee from twice their number. That verse was abrogated, except for this numerical limit.

Al-Kalbi said: Whoever faces the day, advancing or retreating, is a martyr, but the one who advances has preceded the one who retreats into Paradise.

Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: A man fled from (the battle of) al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I have fled from the battle." 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: "I am your group (*fi'ah*)."

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: When Abu 'Ubayd was killed, news reached 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a group for him [so I am a group for every Muslim]."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: We were at Masil, [where] the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent us out. The people charged into a rout, and we fled. We said: "We will flee into the land out of shame at what we have done," and we entered the houses.

Then we said: "O Messenger of God, we are the fleeing ones." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the ones who return to the attack, and we are the group of the Muslims."

[220] [Bada'i' al-Sana'i': 7/99; al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya: 4/283.]

Others said: Rather, our ruling is general, applying to everyone who turns his back on the enemy. Among them is one who narrated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to some of his family: "Beware of fleeing from the battle, for if they perish, then stand firm, for [...]" except in the case of committing major sins, and except for polytheism with God, and fleeing from the battle, because God Most High says: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse).

﴿فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ﴾ (the verse).

The people of tafsir and of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived at Badr, he said: "These are the places where the people will fall, God willing." When they [the polytheists] came into view, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is Quraysh; they have come with their arrogance and pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Gabriel came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them."

When the two hosts met, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley." He handed him pebbles mixed with dust, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw them into the faces of the people and said: "May the faces be disfigured (*shāhat al-wujūh*)."

No polytheist remained who did not get some of it in his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils. Then the believers pursued them, killing and capturing them, and that throw was the cause of the rout. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/270–271.]

Hakim ibn Hizam said: On the day of Badr we heard a sound fall from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw that throw, and we fled.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took three pebbles on the day of Badr: he threw one pebble at the right wing of the enemy, one at their left wing, and one in the midst of them, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and they fled. [222] [Ibid.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it, and said: "O Muhammad, will God give life to this when it is decayed?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will cause you to enter the Fire." When the day of Badr came, he [Ubayy] was taken prisoner, then he was ransomed. When he had been ransomed, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have a horse that I feed a *faraq* of grain every day, so that I may kill you upon it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing."

When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf came charging on that horse until he drew close to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Step back (*istākhirū*)!" They stepped back. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up with a spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The spear broke and struck one of his ribs, and Ubayy returned to his companions, heavy [with the wound]. They carried him and began saying: "There is no harm." But Ubayy said: "By God, if it had been spread among the people, it would have killed them all! Did he not say, 'I will kill you, God willing'?" His companions took him away mourning him, until he died at a place along the road. They buried him, and concerning that God revealed this verse: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ (the verse). [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/46.]

Safwan ibn 'Amr narrated from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn [Jubayr] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Khaybar asked for a bow. A long bow was brought to him, and he said: "Bring me something else." They brought him a stiff bow (*qaws kabdā'*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) shot at the fortress. The arrow came down until it killed Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. Then God Most High revealed: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ﴾. This is the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) of the verse. [Asbab al-Nuzul: 156; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/308.]

As for its meaning: God Most High attributed the killing and the throwing to Himself, because from Him, Most High, came the causing and the making accurate (*al-tasbib wa al-tasdid*), and from His Messenger and the believers came the striking and the casting. Likewise all other human acts are acquired from God, who originates and brings them into being through eternal, perfect power, while from creatures comes the acquisition (*al-iktisab*) through created faculties. In this statement there is evidence for the establishment of the doctrine of the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) and the falsity of the view of the Qadariyya.

It was said: He attributed it to Himself only so that the people would not be vain (*li-allā yuʿjaba al-qawm*).

Mujahid said: [The companions] said: "I killed," and another said: "I killed," so God revealed this verse.

Al-Hasan said: He meant: "You did not cause them to die, but God caused them to die, and you wounded them, because the release of the soul is to Him, not to anyone else."

He said: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾, i.e. [killed], reaching the polytheists with it and filling their eyes with it.

Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: that throw was not yours were it not for what God placed in it of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy because of it, until He routed them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning "He gave you victory." Al-A'mash said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: He granted you success and made your throw accurate.

[Author's note: What I have stated is derived from the verse itself; the verse intends to place the strike of the Greatest Messenger in the position of the strike of the Exalted Creator. So although the Messenger is the thrower, God Most High is the thrower, and it is in the force of the famous sacred hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts [and acts of worship] until I love him; when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks." See Ghawali al-La'ali: 4/103 no. 152; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/229 no. 1155.]

﴿وَلِيُبْلِيَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْهُ بَلَاءً حَسَنًا﴾: i.e. and that He might bestow upon the believers a great favour through victory, spoils, reward and recompense.

Ibn Ishaq said: [That He might make the believers know the blessing of their victory and their triumph over their enemy despite their small number and their enemy's great number, so that they would know His right and thank Him for His blessings]. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ﴾ of their words, ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ of their deeds; He hears their secrets and knows their inner thoughts.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾: i.e. what I have mentioned of killing, throwing and the good trial. ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e. and know that God [...]. Concerning the opening of *anna* (the reading with fatha), there are the aspects found in His saying: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ وَأَنَّ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَذَابَ النَّارِ﴾ [and we have explained it there].

﴿مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾: weakening (*mudʿif*) the plotting of the disbelievers. The people of Hijaz, Syria and Basra read *muwahhinun* with tashdid and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative. Most of the people of Kufa read *muhinun* with takhfif and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative, and this was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash and Hafs read *muhinu kaydi*, with light pronunciation and idafa in the genitive. Whoever reads with tanwin means: "weakens." Whoever reads with takhfif and idafa, the lightness is shortened, as in His saying: ﴿مُرْسِلُو النَّاقَةِ﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 27] and ﴿كَاشِفُو الْعَذَابِ﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 15]. *Wahana* and *awhana* are two sound and eloquent dialects.

﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾: This is because Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O God, whichever of us is the more wicked and the more severing of kinship, and has brought what we do not know, give us victory over him." God answered his supplication and brought victory, and the two sons of 'Afra', 'Awf and Mas'ud, struck him, and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud finished him off. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/274.]

Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: When the polytheists set out from Mecca towards the Prophet (ﷺ), they clung to the curtains of the Ka'ba and said: "O God, give us victory over the two parties, guide the two factions, honour the two armies, and favour the two religions." So God revealed this verse.

'Ikrima said: The polytheists said: "O God, we do not know what Muhammad has brought, so judge between us and him in truth." So God revealed: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek a judgement, the judgement has come to you.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: This is an address to the companions of the Messenger of God. God said to the Muslims: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek victory from God and ask Him for conquest, then ﴿فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. with the help.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We complained to the Messenger of God (ʿalayhi al-salām), saying: "Do not seek victory for us." His face reddened, and he said: "A man before you would be seized, a pit would be dug for him in the ground, then a saw would be brought and he would be cut in two; nothing would turn him from his religion. Iron combs would scrape his flesh and sinews down to the bone, and nothing would turn him from his religion. This matter will certainly be completed by God, until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt and fears nothing but God, and the wolf [fears nothing] for his sheep. But you are being hasty." [224] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/109; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 4/63.]

Then He said to the disbelievers: ﴿وَإِنْ تَنْتَهُوا﴾ from disbelief in God and fighting His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to fight him and wage war against him, ﴿نَعُدْ﴾ with the like of the event that befell you on the day of Badr. [Cf. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/387.]

It was said: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to this statement and to fighting Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿وَلَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْكُمْ فِئَتُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ كَثُرَتْ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The people of Medina and Syria [read] *wa-anna Allāha* with the *alif* opened, meaning: "and because God [...]." It was said: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

The rest read it with kasra, as a new sentence (*istiʾnaf*), and they differed concerning it. Abu Hatim's reading is "*li-anna*" (because), and in the reading of 'Abdullah: "and God is with the believers."

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَا تَوَلَّوْا عَنْهُ﴾: do not turn away from His Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ his command, his ally (*waliyyuhu*).

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ the Qur'an and its admonitions. ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا﴾: meaning the hypocrites and the polytheists who heard the Book of God with their ears and said "We have heard," ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning they do not take admonition from the Qur'an, nor benefit from their hearing, as if they had not heard the truth.

O you who believe! When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle), do not turn your backs to them. (﴿إِذَا لَقِيتُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا زَحْفًا فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾)

*Zahfan* means: [defeated] drawing close to one another, (i.e.) some of you approaching others. *Al-tazahhuf* (the drawing near and converging of two armies) means drawing close and coming near.

Al-A'sha said:

"For whom are the enmities? Their march is a rumbling, like a great ship that is tossed about when the tossing begins."

*Al-zahf* is a verbal noun (masdar), which is why it is not pluralised, as in their saying: "a just people" (qawm 'adl) and "a satisfied people" (qawm ridan).

﴿فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾ means: do not turn your backs to them so that you flee from them, but stand firm against them.

﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾: [whoever turns his back to them on that day], i.e. his back. Al-Hasan read *dubura* with a sukun (dubur).

﴿إِلَّا مُتَحَرِّفًا لِقِتَالٍ﴾: i.e. one who swerves (*mutaʿattifan*) or withdraws (*mustaṭriden*) for battle, by seeking an opening in his enemy that will enable him to strike him, and so he turns back upon him. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/265.]

﴿أَوْ مُتَحَيِّزًا﴾: i.e. one who joins (*munḍammun*) and remains steadfast, ﴿إِلَى فِئَةٍ﴾: a group of believers who will rally to him so that he may return to the fight. ﴿فَقَدْ بَاءَ بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمَأْوَاهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the ruling of His saying ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse): whether it is specific to the people of Badr or applies to all believers.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: This applied only on the day of Badr. They were not permitted to withdraw, even to join the polytheists. On that day there was no Muslim on earth other than them, and the Muslims had no one [to rally to] except the Prophet (ﷺ). But after that, the Muslims are a group [who rally] to one another, [as in] the one "composed" (of a unified force). This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatada.

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: God made the Fire obligatory for whoever fled on the day of Badr, and He said: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse). Then, when the day of Uhud came after that, He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا اسْتَزَلَّهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا كَسَبُوا وَلَقَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 155]. Then the day of Hunayn came seven years later, and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ﴾ ... ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 25–27].

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: This verse was abrogated (*mansukha*, see *naskh* – abrogation) by His saying: ﴿الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 66] and what follows. So it is not permitted for a people to flee from twice their number. That verse was abrogated, except for this numerical limit.

Al-Kalbi said: Whoever faces the day, advancing or retreating, is a martyr, but the one who advances has preceded the one who retreats into Paradise.

Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: A man fled from (the battle of) al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I have fled from the battle." 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: "I am your group (*fi'ah*)."

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: When Abu 'Ubayd was killed, news reached 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a group for him [so I am a group for every Muslim]."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: We were at Masil, [where] the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent us out. The people charged into a rout, and we fled. We said: "We will flee into the land out of shame at what we have done," and we entered the houses.

Then we said: "O Messenger of God, we are the fleeing ones." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the ones who return to the attack, and we are the group of the Muslims."

[220] [Bada'i' al-Sana'i': 7/99; al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya: 4/283.]

Others said: Rather, our ruling is general, applying to everyone who turns his back on the enemy. Among them is one who narrated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to some of his family: "Beware of fleeing from the battle, for if they perish, then stand firm, for [...]" except in the case of committing major sins, and except for polytheism with God, and fleeing from the battle, because God Most High says: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse).

﴿فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ﴾ (the verse).

The people of tafsir and of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived at Badr, he said: "These are the places where the people will fall, God willing." When they [the polytheists] came into view, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is Quraysh; they have come with their arrogance and pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Gabriel came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them."

When the two hosts met, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley." He handed him pebbles mixed with dust, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw them into the faces of the people and said: "May the faces be disfigured (*shāhat al-wujūh*)."

No polytheist remained who did not get some of it in his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils. Then the believers pursued them, killing and capturing them, and that throw was the cause of the rout. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/270–271.]

Hakim ibn Hizam said: On the day of Badr we heard a sound fall from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw that throw, and we fled.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took three pebbles on the day of Badr: he threw one pebble at the right wing of the enemy, one at their left wing, and one in the midst of them, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and they fled. [222] [Ibid.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it, and said: "O Muhammad, will God give life to this when it is decayed?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will cause you to enter the Fire." When the day of Badr came, he [Ubayy] was taken prisoner, then he was ransomed. When he had been ransomed, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have a horse that I feed a *faraq* of grain every day, so that I may kill you upon it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing."

When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf came charging on that horse until he drew close to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Step back (*istākhirū*)!" They stepped back. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up with a spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The spear broke and struck one of his ribs, and Ubayy returned to his companions, heavy [with the wound]. They carried him and began saying: "There is no harm." But Ubayy said: "By God, if it had been spread among the people, it would have killed them all! Did he not say, 'I will kill you, God willing'?" His companions took him away mourning him, until he died at a place along the road. They buried him, and concerning that God revealed this verse: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ (the verse). [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/46.]

Safwan ibn 'Amr narrated from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn [Jubayr] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Khaybar asked for a bow. A long bow was brought to him, and he said: "Bring me something else." They brought him a stiff bow (*qaws kabdā'*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) shot at the fortress. The arrow came down until it killed Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. Then God Most High revealed: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ﴾. This is the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) of the verse. [Asbab al-Nuzul: 156; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/308.]

As for its meaning: God Most High attributed the killing and the throwing to Himself, because from Him, Most High, came the causing and the making accurate (*al-tasbib wa al-tasdid*), and from His Messenger and the believers came the striking and the casting. Likewise all other human acts are acquired from God, who originates and brings them into being through eternal, perfect power, while from creatures comes the acquisition (*al-iktisab*) through created faculties. In this statement there is evidence for the establishment of the doctrine of the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) and the falsity of the view of the Qadariyya.

It was said: He attributed it to Himself only so that the people would not be vain (*li-allā yuʿjaba al-qawm*).

Mujahid said: [The companions] said: "I killed," and another said: "I killed," so God revealed this verse.

Al-Hasan said: He meant: "You did not cause them to die, but God caused them to die, and you wounded them, because the release of the soul is to Him, not to anyone else."

He said: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾, i.e. [killed], reaching the polytheists with it and filling their eyes with it.

Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: that throw was not yours were it not for what God placed in it of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy because of it, until He routed them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning "He gave you victory." Al-A'mash said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: He granted you success and made your throw accurate.

[Author's note: What I have stated is derived from the verse itself; the verse intends to place the strike of the Greatest Messenger in the position of the strike of the Exalted Creator. So although the Messenger is the thrower, God Most High is the thrower, and it is in the force of the famous sacred hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts [and acts of worship] until I love him; when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks." See Ghawali al-La'ali: 4/103 no. 152; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/229 no. 1155.]

﴿وَلِيُبْلِيَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْهُ بَلَاءً حَسَنًا﴾: i.e. and that He might bestow upon the believers a great favour through victory, spoils, reward and recompense.

Ibn Ishaq said: [That He might make the believers know the blessing of their victory and their triumph over their enemy despite their small number and their enemy's great number, so that they would know His right and thank Him for His blessings]. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ﴾ of their words, ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ of their deeds; He hears their secrets and knows their inner thoughts.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾: i.e. what I have mentioned of killing, throwing and the good trial. ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e. and know that God [...]. Concerning the opening of *anna* (the reading with fatha), there are the aspects found in His saying: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ وَأَنَّ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَذَابَ النَّارِ﴾ [and we have explained it there].

﴿مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾: weakening (*mudʿif*) the plotting of the disbelievers. The people of Hijaz, Syria and Basra read *muwahhinun* with tashdid and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative. Most of the people of Kufa read *muhinun* with takhfif and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative, and this was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash and Hafs read *muhinu kaydi*, with light pronunciation and idafa in the genitive. Whoever reads with tanwin means: "weakens." Whoever reads with takhfif and idafa, the lightness is shortened, as in His saying: ﴿مُرْسِلُو النَّاقَةِ﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 27] and ﴿كَاشِفُو الْعَذَابِ﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 15]. *Wahana* and *awhana* are two sound and eloquent dialects.

﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾: This is because Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O God, whichever of us is the more wicked and the more severing of kinship, and has brought what we do not know, give us victory over him." God answered his supplication and brought victory, and the two sons of 'Afra', 'Awf and Mas'ud, struck him, and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud finished him off. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/274.]

Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: When the polytheists set out from Mecca towards the Prophet (ﷺ), they clung to the curtains of the Ka'ba and said: "O God, give us victory over the two parties, guide the two factions, honour the two armies, and favour the two religions." So God revealed this verse.

'Ikrima said: The polytheists said: "O God, we do not know what Muhammad has brought, so judge between us and him in truth." So God revealed: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek a judgement, the judgement has come to you.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: This is an address to the companions of the Messenger of God. God said to the Muslims: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek victory from God and ask Him for conquest, then ﴿فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. with the help.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We complained to the Messenger of God (ʿalayhi al-salām), saying: "Do not seek victory for us." His face reddened, and he said: "A man before you would be seized, a pit would be dug for him in the ground, then a saw would be brought and he would be cut in two; nothing would turn him from his religion. Iron combs would scrape his flesh and sinews down to the bone, and nothing would turn him from his religion. This matter will certainly be completed by God, until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt and fears nothing but God, and the wolf [fears nothing] for his sheep. But you are being hasty." [224] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/109; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 4/63.]

Then He said to the disbelievers: ﴿وَإِنْ تَنْتَهُوا﴾ from disbelief in God and fighting His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to fight him and wage war against him, ﴿نَعُدْ﴾ with the like of the event that befell you on the day of Badr. [Cf. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/387.]

It was said: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to this statement and to fighting Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿وَلَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْكُمْ فِئَتُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ كَثُرَتْ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The people of Medina and Syria [read] *wa-anna Allāha* with the *alif* opened, meaning: "and because God [...]." It was said: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

The rest read it with kasra, as a new sentence (*istiʾnaf*), and they differed concerning it. Abu Hatim's reading is "*li-anna*" (because), and in the reading of 'Abdullah: "and God is with the believers."

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَا تَوَلَّوْا عَنْهُ﴾: do not turn away from His Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ his command, his ally (*waliyyuhu*).

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ the Qur'an and its admonitions. ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا﴾: meaning the hypocrites and the polytheists who heard the Book of God with their ears and said "We have heard," ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning they do not take admonition from the Qur'an, nor benefit from their hearing, as if they had not heard the truth.

O you who believe! When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle), do not turn your backs to them. (﴿إِذَا لَقِيتُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا زَحْفًا فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾)

*Zahfan* means: [defeated] drawing close to one another, (i.e.) some of you approaching others. *Al-tazahhuf* (the drawing near and converging of two armies) means drawing close and coming near.

Al-A'sha said:

"For whom are the enmities? Their march is a rumbling, like a great ship that is tossed about when the tossing begins."

*Al-zahf* is a verbal noun (masdar), which is why it is not pluralised, as in their saying: "a just people" (qawm 'adl) and "a satisfied people" (qawm ridan).

﴿فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾ means: do not turn your backs to them so that you flee from them, but stand firm against them.

﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾: [whoever turns his back to them on that day], i.e. his back. Al-Hasan read *dubura* with a sukun (dubur).

﴿إِلَّا مُتَحَرِّفًا لِقِتَالٍ﴾: i.e. one who swerves (*mutaʿattifan*) or withdraws (*mustaṭriden*) for battle, by seeking an opening in his enemy that will enable him to strike him, and so he turns back upon him. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/265.]

﴿أَوْ مُتَحَيِّزًا﴾: i.e. one who joins (*munḍammun*) and remains steadfast, ﴿إِلَى فِئَةٍ﴾: a group of believers who will rally to him so that he may return to the fight. ﴿فَقَدْ بَاءَ بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمَأْوَاهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the ruling of His saying ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse): whether it is specific to the people of Badr or applies to all believers.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: This applied only on the day of Badr. They were not permitted to withdraw, even to join the polytheists. On that day there was no Muslim on earth other than them, and the Muslims had no one [to rally to] except the Prophet (ﷺ). But after that, the Muslims are a group [who rally] to one another, [as in] the one "composed" (of a unified force). This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatada.

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: God made the Fire obligatory for whoever fled on the day of Badr, and He said: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse). Then, when the day of Uhud came after that, He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا اسْتَزَلَّهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا كَسَبُوا وَلَقَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 155]. Then the day of Hunayn came seven years later, and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ﴾ ... ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 25–27].

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: This verse was abrogated (*mansukha*, see *naskh* – abrogation) by His saying: ﴿الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 66] and what follows. So it is not permitted for a people to flee from twice their number. That verse was abrogated, except for this numerical limit.

Al-Kalbi said: Whoever faces the day, advancing or retreating, is a martyr, but the one who advances has preceded the one who retreats into Paradise.

Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: A man fled from (the battle of) al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I have fled from the battle." 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: "I am your group (*fi'ah*)."

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: When Abu 'Ubayd was killed, news reached 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a group for him [so I am a group for every Muslim]."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: We were at Masil, [where] the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent us out. The people charged into a rout, and we fled. We said: "We will flee into the land out of shame at what we have done," and we entered the houses.

Then we said: "O Messenger of God, we are the fleeing ones." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the ones who return to the attack, and we are the group of the Muslims."

[220] [Bada'i' al-Sana'i': 7/99; al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya: 4/283.]

Others said: Rather, our ruling is general, applying to everyone who turns his back on the enemy. Among them is one who narrated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to some of his family: "Beware of fleeing from the battle, for if they perish, then stand firm, for [...]" except in the case of committing major sins, and except for polytheism with God, and fleeing from the battle, because God Most High says: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse).

﴿فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ﴾ (the verse).

The people of tafsir and of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived at Badr, he said: "These are the places where the people will fall, God willing." When they [the polytheists] came into view, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is Quraysh; they have come with their arrogance and pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Gabriel came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them."

When the two hosts met, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley." He handed him pebbles mixed with dust, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw them into the faces of the people and said: "May the faces be disfigured (*shāhat al-wujūh*)."

No polytheist remained who did not get some of it in his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils. Then the believers pursued them, killing and capturing them, and that throw was the cause of the rout. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/270–271.]

Hakim ibn Hizam said: On the day of Badr we heard a sound fall from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw that throw, and we fled.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took three pebbles on the day of Badr: he threw one pebble at the right wing of the enemy, one at their left wing, and one in the midst of them, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and they fled. [222] [Ibid.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it, and said: "O Muhammad, will God give life to this when it is decayed?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will cause you to enter the Fire." When the day of Badr came, he [Ubayy] was taken prisoner, then he was ransomed. When he had been ransomed, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have a horse that I feed a *faraq* of grain every day, so that I may kill you upon it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing."

When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf came charging on that horse until he drew close to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Step back (*istākhirū*)!" They stepped back. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up with a spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The spear broke and struck one of his ribs, and Ubayy returned to his companions, heavy [with the wound]. They carried him and began saying: "There is no harm." But Ubayy said: "By God, if it had been spread among the people, it would have killed them all! Did he not say, 'I will kill you, God willing'?" His companions took him away mourning him, until he died at a place along the road. God answered his supplication and brought victory, and the two sons of 'Afra', 'Awf and Mas'ud, struck him, and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud finished him off. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/274.]

Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: When the polytheists set out from Mecca towards the Prophet (ﷺ), they clung to the curtains of the Ka'ba and said: "O God, give us victory over the two parties, guide the two factions, honour the two armies, and favour the two religions." So God revealed this verse.

'Ikrima said: The polytheists said: "O God, we do not know what Muhammad has brought, so judge between us and him in truth." So God revealed: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek a judgement, the judgement has come to you.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: This is an address to the companions of the Messenger of God. God said to the Muslims: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek victory from God and ask Him for conquest, then ﴿فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. with the help.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We complained to the Messenger of God (ʿalayhi al-salām), saying: "Do not seek victory for us." His face reddened, and he said: "A man before you would be seized, a pit would be dug for him in the ground, then a saw would be brought and he would be cut in two; nothing would turn him from his religion. Iron combs would scrape his flesh and sinews down to the bone, and nothing would turn him from his religion. This matter will certainly be completed by God, until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt and fears nothing but God, and the wolf [fears nothing] for his sheep. But you are being hasty." [224] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/109; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 4/63.]

Then He said to the disbelievers: ﴿وَإِنْ تَنْتَهُوا﴾ from disbelief in God and fighting His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to fight him and wage war against him, ﴿نَعُدْ﴾ with the like of the event that befell you on the day of Badr. [Cf. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/387.]

It was said: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to this statement and to fighting Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿وَلَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْكُمْ فِئَتُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ كَثُرَتْ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The people of Medina and Syria [read] *wa-anna Allāha* with the *alif* opened, meaning: "and because God [...]." It was said: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

The rest read it with kasra, as a new sentence (*istiʾnaf*), and they differed concerning it. Abu Hatim's reading is "*li-anna*" (because), and in the reading of 'Abdullah: "and God is with the believers."

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَا تَوَلَّوْا عَنْهُ﴾: do not turn away from His Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ his command, his ally (*waliyyuhu*).

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ the Qur'an and its admonitions. ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا﴾: meaning the hypocrites and the polytheists who heard the Book of God with their ears and said "We have heard," ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning they do not take admonition from the Qur'an, nor benefit from their hearing, as if they had not heard the truth.

O you who believe! When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (for battle), do not turn your backs to them. (﴿إِذَا لَقِيتُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا زَحْفًا فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾)

*Zahfan* means: [defeated] drawing close to one another, (i.e.) some of you approaching others. *Al-tazahhuf* (the drawing near and converging of two armies) means drawing close and coming near.

Al-A'sha said:

"For whom are the enmities? Their march is a rumbling, like a great ship that is tossed about when the tossing begins."

*Al-zahf* is a verbal noun (masdar), which is why it is not pluralised, as in their saying: "a just people" (qawm 'adl) and "a satisfied people" (qawm ridan).

﴿فَلَا تُوَلُّوهُمُ الْأَدْبَارَ﴾ means: do not turn your backs to them so that you flee from them, but stand firm against them.

﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾: [whoever turns his back to them on that day], i.e. his back. Al-Hasan read *dubura* with a sukun (dubur).

﴿إِلَّا مُتَحَرِّفًا لِقِتَالٍ﴾: i.e. one who swerves (*mutaʿattifan*) or withdraws (*mustaṭriden*) for battle, by seeking an opening in his enemy that will enable him to strike him, and so he turns back upon him. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/265.]

﴿أَوْ مُتَحَيِّزًا﴾: i.e. one who joins (*munḍammun*) and remains steadfast, ﴿إِلَى فِئَةٍ﴾: a group of believers who will rally to him so that he may return to the fight. ﴿فَقَدْ بَاءَ بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمَأْوَاهُ جَهَنَّمُ وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the ruling of His saying ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse): whether it is specific to the people of Badr or applies to all believers.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: This applied only on the day of Badr. They were not permitted to withdraw, even to join the polytheists. On that day there was no Muslim on earth other than them, and the Muslims had no one [to rally to] except the Prophet (ﷺ). But after that, the Muslims are a group [who rally] to one another, [as in] the one "composed" (of a unified force). This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatada.

Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: God made the Fire obligatory for whoever fled on the day of Badr, and He said: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse). Then, when the day of Uhud came after that, He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا اسْتَزَلَّهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا كَسَبُوا وَلَقَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 155]. Then the day of Hunayn came seven years later, and He said: ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ﴾ ... ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 25–27].

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: This verse was abrogated (*mansukha*, see *naskh* – abrogation) by His saying: ﴿الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 66] and what follows. So it is not permitted for a people to flee from twice their number. That verse was abrogated, except for this numerical limit.

Al-Kalbi said: Whoever faces the day, advancing or retreating, is a martyr, but the one who advances has preceded the one who retreats into Paradise.

Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: A man fled from (the battle of) al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I have fled from the battle." 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: "I am your group (*fi'ah*)."

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: When Abu 'Ubayd was killed, news reached 'Umar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a group for him [so I am a group for every Muslim]."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: We were at Masil, [where] the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent us out. The people charged into a rout, and we fled. We said: "We will flee into the land out of shame at what we have done," and we entered the houses.

Then we said: "O Messenger of God, we are the fleeing ones." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the ones who return to the attack, and we are the group of the Muslims."

[220] [Bada'i' al-Sana'i': 7/99; al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya: 4/283.]

Others said: Rather, our ruling is general, applying to everyone who turns his back on the enemy. Among them is one who narrated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to some of his family: "Beware of fleeing from the battle, for if they perish, then stand firm, for [...]" except in the case of committing major sins, and except for polytheism with God, and fleeing from the battle, because God Most High says: ﴿وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ (the verse).

﴿فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ﴾ (the verse).

The people of tafsir and of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived at Badr, he said: "These are the places where the people will fall, God willing." When they [the polytheists] came into view, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is Quraysh; they have come with their arrogance and pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me." Then Gabriel came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them."

When the two hosts met, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley." He handed him pebbles mixed with dust, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw them into the faces of the people and said: "May the faces be disfigured (*shāhat al-wujūh*)."

No polytheist remained who did not get some of it in his eyes, his mouth and his nostrils. Then the believers pursued them, killing and capturing them, and that throw was the cause of the rout. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/270–271.]

Hakim ibn Hizam said: On the day of Badr we heard a sound fall from the sky, as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw that throw, and we fled.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took three pebbles on the day of Badr: he threw one pebble at the right wing of the enemy, one at their left wing, and one in the midst of them, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and they fled. [222] [Ibid.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbling it, and said: "O Muhammad, will God give life to this when it is decayed?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will cause you to enter the Fire." When the day of Badr came, he [Ubayy] was taken prisoner, then he was ransomed. When he had been ransomed, he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have a horse that I feed a *faraq* of grain every day, so that I may kill you upon it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing."

When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf came charging on that horse until he drew close to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Step back (*istākhirū*)!" They stepped back. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up with a spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The spear broke and struck one of his ribs, and Ubayy returned to his companions, heavy [with the wound]. They carried him and began saying: "There is no harm." But Ubayy said: "By God, if it had been spread among the people, it would have killed them all! Did he not say, 'I will kill you, God willing'?" His companions took him away mourning him, until he died at a place along the road. They buried him, and concerning that God revealed this verse: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ (the verse). [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/46.]

Safwan ibn 'Amr narrated from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn [Jubayr] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Khaybar asked for a bow. A long bow was brought to him, and he said: "Bring me something else." They brought him a stiff bow (*qaws kabdā'*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) shot at the fortress. The arrow came down until it killed Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. Then God Most High revealed: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ﴾. This is the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) of the verse. [Asbab al-Nuzul: 156; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/308.]

As for its meaning: God Most High attributed the killing and the throwing to Himself, because from Him, Most High, came the causing and the making accurate (*al-tasbib wa al-tasdid*), and from His Messenger and the believers came the striking and the casting. Likewise all other human acts are acquired from God, who originates and brings them into being through eternal, perfect power, while from creatures comes the acquisition (*al-iktisab*) through created faculties. In this statement there is evidence for the establishment of the doctrine of the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) and the falsity of the view of the Qadariyya.

It was said: He attributed it to Himself only so that the people would not be vain (*li-allā yuʿjaba al-qawm*).

Mujahid said: [The companions] said: "I killed," and another said: "I killed," so God revealed this verse.

Al-Hasan said: He meant: "You did not cause them to die, but God caused them to die, and you wounded them, because the release of the soul is to Him, not to anyone else."

He said: ﴿وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾, i.e. [killed], reaching the polytheists with it and filling their eyes with it.

Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: that throw was not yours were it not for what God placed in it of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy because of it, until He routed them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning "He gave you victory." Al-A'mash said: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَى﴾ means: He granted you success and made your throw accurate.

[Author's note: What I have stated is derived from the verse itself; the verse intends to place the strike of the Greatest Messenger in the position of the strike of the Exalted Creator. So although the Messenger is the thrower, God Most High is the thrower, and it is in the force of the famous sacred hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts [and acts of worship] until I love him; when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks." See Ghawali al-La'ali: 4/103 no. 152; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/229 no. 1155.]

﴿وَلِيُبْلِيَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْهُ بَلَاءً حَسَنًا﴾: i.e. and that He might bestow upon the believers a great favour through victory, spoils, reward and recompense.

Ibn Ishaq said: [That He might make the believers know the blessing of their victory and their triumph over their enemy despite their small number and their enemy's great number, so that they would know His right and thank Him for His blessings]. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ﴾ of their words, ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ of their deeds; He hears their secrets and knows their inner thoughts.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾: i.e. what I have mentioned of killing, throwing and the good trial. ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e. and know that God [...]. Concerning the opening of *anna* (the reading with fatha), there are the aspects found in His saying: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ وَأَنَّ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَذَابَ النَّارِ﴾ [and we have explained it there].

﴿مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾: weakening (*mudʿif*) the plotting of the disbelievers. The people of Hijaz, Syria and Basra read *muwahhinun* with tashdid and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative. Most of the people of Kufa read *muhinun* with takhfif and tanwin, with *kayda* in the accusative, and this was chosen by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash and Hafs read *muhinu kaydi*, with light pronunciation and idafa in the genitive. Whoever reads with tanwin means: "weakens." Whoever reads with takhfif and idafa, the lightness is shortened, as in His saying: ﴿مُرْسِلُو النَّاقَةِ﴾ [Surah al-Qamar: 27] and ﴿كَاشِفُو الْعَذَابِ﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 15]. *Wahana* and *awhana* are two sound and eloquent dialects.

﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾: This is because Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O God, whichever of us is the more wicked and the more severing of kinship, and has brought what we do not know, give us victory over him." God answered his supplication and brought victory, and the two sons of 'Afra', 'Awf and Mas'ud, struck him, and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud finished him off. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/274.]

Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: When the polytheists set out from Mecca towards the Prophet (ﷺ), they clung to the curtains of the Ka'ba and said: "O God, give us victory over the two parties, guide the two factions, honour the two armies, and favour the two religions." So God revealed this verse.

'Ikrima said: The polytheists said: "O God, we do not know what Muhammad has brought, so judge between us and him in truth." So God revealed: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek a judgement, the judgement has come to you.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: This is an address to the companions of the Messenger of God. God said to the Muslims: ﴿إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. if you seek victory from God and ask Him for conquest, then ﴿فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ﴾, i.e. with the help.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We complained to the Messenger of God (ʿalayhi al-salām), saying: "Do not seek victory for us." His face reddened, and he said: "A man before you would be seized, a pit would be dug for him in the ground, then a saw would be brought and he would be cut in two; nothing would turn him from his religion. Iron combs would scrape his flesh and sinews down to the bone, and nothing would turn him from his religion. This matter will certainly be completed by God, until a rider travels from Sana'a to Hadramawt and fears nothing but God, and the wolf [fears nothing] for his sheep. But you are being hasty." [224] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/109; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 4/63.]

Then He said to the disbelievers: ﴿وَإِنْ تَنْتَهُوا﴾ from disbelief in God and fighting His Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to fight him and wage war against him, ﴿نَعُدْ﴾ with the like of the event that befell you on the day of Badr. [Cf. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 7/387.]

It was said: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا﴾ to this statement and to fighting Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿وَلَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْكُمْ فِئَتُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ كَثُرَتْ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The people of Medina and Syria [read] *wa-anna Allāha* with the *alif* opened, meaning: "and because God [...]." It was said: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مُوهِنُ كَيْدِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

The rest read it with kasra, as a new sentence (*istiʾnaf*), and they differed concerning it. Abu Hatim's reading is "*li-anna*" (because), and in the reading of 'Abdullah: "and God is with the believers."

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَا تَوَلَّوْا عَنْهُ﴾: do not turn away from His Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ his command, his ally (*waliyyuhu*).

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تَسْمَعُونَ﴾ the Qur'an and its admonitions. ﴿وَلَا تَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا﴾: meaning the hypocrites and the polytheists who heard the Book of God with their ears and said "We have heard," ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: meaning they do not take admonition from the Qur'an, nor benefit from their hearing, as if they had not heard the truth.

**Al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan), commentary on Surah 8, verses 22–26:**

﴿Indeed, the worst of the creatures (al-dawabb)﴾, meaning: the worst [creatures] [dawabb] on the face of the earth, in the sight of God. Al-Akhfash said: every creature in need of nourishment is a *dabbah* (creature/beast).

﴿The deaf and the dumb﴾ from the truth, as if they neither hear nor speak.

Ibn Zayd said: they are deaf of heart, dumb of heart, and blind of heart. He recited: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46].

Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah said: they are the Bani Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy. They used to say, "We are deaf, dumb, and blind to the address of Muhammad: we do not hear him and we do not answer him." [They] were all [killed] [at Uhud], and they were the standard-bearers. Of them, none embraced Islam except two men: Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Suwaybit ibn Harmala.

﴿Who do not understand the command of God.﴾ ﴿And if God had known any good in them﴾, meaning truthfulness and Islam, ﴿He would have made them hear﴾, meaning He would have granted them understanding and knowledge of the Qur'an. ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away﴾ from the Qur'an, ﴿being averse﴾, refusing to believe in the Qur'an, because of God's knowledge concerning them and His judgment upon them as disbelievers.

﴿O you who believe! Respond to God and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾. The scholars differed concerning His words ﴿that which gives you life﴾:

Al-Suddi said: it is faith, which gives them life after their death, that is, their disbelief. Mujahid said: it is the truth. Qatadah said: it is this Qur'an, in which there is life, understanding, salvation, and protection in this world and the Hereafter.

Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿that which gives you life﴾ means war and jihad, through which God honored you after humiliation, strengthened you after weakness, and protected you through them from your enemy after they had overpowered you.

He commanded them and then forbade them, and in it is the sense of a conditional, and its implied meaning is: "Fear God, lest if you do not desist, it will befall you."

Al-Kisa'i said: the *nun* appears in the place of warning in the jussive. If you say, "Stand up, I will not be angry with you," there would be no *nun*, because it is a pure conditional.

Al-Farra' said: it is a conditional with an element of prohibition, as you say, "Get down from the animal, it will not throw you," and "it will not throw you" (la yatrahannaka): this is a conditional in the form of a command expressed as a prohibition. Its meaning is: if you get down from it, it will not throw you.

Ibn Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ specifically. He said: God commanded the believers not to tolerate wrongdoing among them, lest God afflict them all with punishment.

Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning Ali, Ammar, Talhah, and al-Zubayr. Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam said on the day of the Camel: "We recited this verse for a time, and we did not think we were among its people, but there we were, the ones it was about." ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike those of you who have done wrong in particular.﴾ So we swore, until it struck us in particular.

Al-Suddi said: this verse was revealed specifically concerning the people of Badr, and it struck them on the day of the Camel, so they turned back.

Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: there is none of you but who is involved in trial. God says: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Anfal 8:28]. So whoever of you seeks refuge, let him seek refuge in God from the misleading trials.

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There will be among my companions some who commit sins which God will forgive them because of their companionship with me, but after them there will be people who follow their example in them, whom God will punish, and He will admit them into the Fire because of them." [227] [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/234.]

Yahya ibn Abd Allah related from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The Hour will not come until a trial, blind and dark, comes, in which the one lying down is better than the one sitting, the one sitting is better than the one standing, the one standing is better than the one walking, and the one walking is better than the one running." [Up to here in Musnad Ahmad: 5/39.]

A man from the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "O Messenger of God, if it reaches me [while I am lying down]?" He said:

"Then walk."

He said: "What if it reaches me while I am walking?" He said: "Then sit still." He said: "What if it reaches me while I am sitting still?" He said: "Then sit still." (Note: the wording of the source is "What if it reaches me while I am sleeping, and I stand up?")

He said: "Then strike with your hand like this," and he gathered his hands to his body, "until you are the wronged one before God and not the wrongdoer before God." [228]

Related from Zayd ibn Abi Ziyad, from Zayd ibn al-Asamm, from Hudhayfah, who said: Trials will come upon you like pieces of the dark night, in which every brave hero will perish, and every rider who is weak, and every eloquent preacher.

﴿And remember when you were few in number﴾, meaning in numbers, ﴿oppressed in the land﴾, the land of Makkah at the beginning of Islam, ﴿fearing that the people would snatch you away﴾, meaning the people would take you off, the disbelievers of Makkah. Wahb said: Persia and Rome. ﴿So He sheltered you in Madinah, and strengthened you with His help﴾ on the day of Badr, strengthening your hands with victory, and reinforcing you with the angels, ﴿and provided you with good things﴾, meaning the spoils, which He made lawful for you and did not make lawful for anyone before you, ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾.

Qatadah said: this tribe of the Arabs was the most humiliated of people in humiliation, the most wretched in life, the hungriest in belly, the barest in skins, and the most misguided. Whoever lived among them lived in misery, and whoever died among them perished into the Fire, [and they were] bound upon the two great stones, Persia and Rome. They were eaten and did not eat, and there was nothing in their lands about which they were envied. By God, we do not know of any tribe from among the settled peoples of the earth at that time that was worse in dwelling than they were, until God, Mighty and Majestic, brought Islam, and He established them in the lands, widened their provision through it, and made you kings over the necks of the people.

Through Islam God gave you what you see, so be thankful to God for His blessings, for your Lord is Bountiful, deserving of gratitude, and [the best] gratitude is in the increase from God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 8, verse 27–31:

O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: Jabir ibn Abdullah narrated to me that Abu Sufyan set out from Makkah, and Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Abu Sufyan is at such-and-such a place."

So the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his companions: "Abu Sufyan is at such-and-such a place, so go out to him, and keep it secret." [229] He said: A man among the hypocrites wrote to them, "Muhammad intends to attack you, so take your precautions." So Allah the Exalted revealed the verse. [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 9/291.]]

And al-Suddi said: They would hear something from the Prophet (ﷺ) and then spread it, until it reached the polytheists.

Al-Zuhri and al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah, whose name was Harun ibn Abd al-Mundhir al-Ansari, of the Banu Awf ibn Malik. This was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged the Jews of Qurayzah for twenty-one nights. They asked the Messenger of Allah for a settlement on the same terms that their brothers, the Banu al-Nadir, had accepted, on condition that they might go to their brothers at Adhri'at and Jericho in the land of Syria. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused to grant them that, except that they should submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. They refused and said: "Send Abu Lubabah ibn Abd al-Mundhir to us," for he was a counsellor to them, because his dependents, his property and his children were with them. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him, and he came to them. They said: "O Abu Lubabah, what do you think? Should we submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh?" Abu Lubabah pointed with his hand to his throat, indicating that it meant slaughter. He said: "Do not do it."

Abu Lubabah said: "By Allah, my feet did not move from their place until I knew that I had betrayed Allah and the Messenger." When this verse was revealed, he bound himself to one of the pillars of the mosque and said: "By Allah, I will not taste food or drink until I die or Allah forgives me." He remained for seven days, tasting no food or drink, until he fell unconscious. Then Allah forgave him. It was said to him: "O Abu Lubabah, Allah has forgiven you."

He said: "No, by Allah, I will not release myself until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the one who releases me." So he came to him, and he untied him with his own hand. Then Abu Lubabah said: "Part of the completion of my repentance is that I abandon the house of my people in which I committed the sin, and that I strip myself of my property." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A third will suffice you if you give it in charity." [230] [[See Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 9/292. It is well known that Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet, peace be upon them both, came to release him, but he refused, and the Messenger of Allah said: "Fatimah is a part of me," and so he was released. See 'Umdat al-Akhbar: 99, chapter four, section on the virtue of the noble mosque; al-Rawd al-Anf of al-Suhayli: 1/160, Book of the Mission, section on his saying to Khadijah: "Jibril conveys his greetings to you"; and 2/196, section on the report of Abu Lubabah.]]

Al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him. [[The same source.]]

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The meaning of the verse is: do not show him the truth that pleases him from you, and then oppose him in secret by turning to something else.

Ibn Abbas said: "Do not betray Allah" by abandoning His obligations, "and the Messenger" by abandoning his sunnah, "and do not betray your trusts."

Al-Suddi said: If they betray Allah and the Messenger, they have betrayed their trusts.

According to this interpretation, His saying "and betray" (wa-takhunu) is in the accusative as an answer to the prohibition.

The Arabs put the answer to a prohibition in the accusative, just as it is put in the accusative after the fa'.

It was also said: it is in the accusative by way of sarf (change of construction), as in the words of the poet:

Do not forbid a trait while you yourself practise its like; it is a great disgrace upon you when you do it.

[[In Lisan al-Arab: 7/447, it says: the verse is by al-Mutawakkil al-Laythi, and it is also narrated for Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali.]]

Al-Akhfash said: it is a conjunction with what precedes it of the prohibition, its meaning being: "and do not betray your trusts."

Mujahid recited "amanatikum" in the singular. They differed concerning this [verse]. Ibn Abbas said: it is what is hidden from people's eyes of the obligations of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the deeds over which Allah has entrusted His servants; He says: do not violate them.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of "trusts" here is the religion, and these hypocrites were entrusted by Allah with His religion, but they betrayed it, since they displayed faith and concealed disbelief.

Qatadah said: The religion of Allah is a trust, so render to Allah what He has entrusted you with of His obligations and limits. Whoever has a trust upon him, let him return it to the one who entrusted him with it.

And know that your wealth and your children

are a trial (fitnah), those that are with the Banu Qurayzah; and that with Allah is a great reward. O you who have believed, if you fear Allah

by obeying Him, leaving off His disobedience, and avoiding betrayal of Him, He will grant you a criterion (furqan). Mujahid said: a way out in this world and the Hereafter.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: a way out from doubtful matters in religion. Ikrimah said: deliverance. Al-Dahhak said: clarity. Muqatil said: a rescuer.

Al-Kalbi said: insight. Ibn Ishaq said: a distinction between truth and falsehood, by which Allah makes manifest your truth and extinguishes the falsehood of those who oppose you.

Ibn Zayd said: a discrimination that Allah places in their hearts between truth and falsehood, so that they recognise it and bear witness to it.

Al-furqan is a verbal noun like al-rahman and al-nuqsan.

You say: "faraqtu bayn al-shay' wa-al-shay' afriqu baynahuma farqan, furuqan, wa-furqanan." And He will expiate from you your past sins and forgive you, and Allah is the Lord of great bounty. And when those who disbelieved plotted against you to confine you (liyuthbitūka)—this verse is linked to His saying, the Exalted: "And remember when you were few" [[Surah al-Anfal: 26.]] and "when those who disbelieved plotted against you."

"And when they said: O Allah..." [[Surah al-Anfal: 30–32.]], because this surah is Medinan.

This speech and this plotting took place in Makkah, but Allah the Exalted mentioned them in Medina, as in His saying: "If you do not help him, Allah has indeed helped him" [[Surah al-Tawbah: 40.]]. This plotting, as Ibn Abbas and others among the exegetes mention, was that the Quraysh, when the Ansar had embraced Islam, feared that the affairs of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would grow.

So a group of their elders and senior men gathered in the Dar al-Nadwah to consult about the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Their leaders were Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl, Abu Sufyan, Tu'mah ibn Adi, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, Hakim ibn Hizam and his sons, Munabbih and Nabih, the two sons of al-Hajjaj, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Iblis came to them in the form of an old man. When they saw him they said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am an old man from Najd. I heard of your gathering, so I wanted to attend, and you will not lack opinion and sincere counsel." They said: "Enter," and he entered.

Abu al-Bakhtari said: "As for me, I think you should seize him, imprison him in a room, bind his shackles, seal the door of the room, leave him, and send him his food and drink, and wait for the calamity of fate to befall him until he dies there, as others died before him, such as the poets Zuhayr and al-Nabighah; he is only like one of them."

Then the old man from Najd cried out and said: "Evil is the opinion you have held. You intend to take the man and imprison him, and you will complete his reward, and those around you have heard of him, [so they will soon rise up and snatch him from your hands] [[Addition from Tarikh al-Tabari: 2/98.]] and fight you on his behalf until they take him from you."

They said: "The old man is right." Then Hisham ibn Amr, who was of the Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy, said: "As for me, I think you should load him on a camel and send him out from among you, so that he will not harm you, for whatever befell him will not harm you once he has gone from you, and he will be gone, and his affair will be in others' hands." Iblis said: "Evil is your opinion. You intend to take a man who has corrupted your foolish ones, and send him out to others, who will corrupt them as he corrupted you. Have you not seen the sweetness of his speech, the eloquence of his tongue, and how he captures hearts by what is heard of his talk? By Allah, if you do so, then he will go around to the Arabs and they will gather against you, and then he will come to you and expel you from your lands and kill your nobles."

They said: "By Allah, the old man is right."

Abu Jahl said: "I will certainly advise you with an opinion other than which I see no other: I think we should take one youth from every clan of Quraysh, a strong lad and of noble lineage, then give each one of them a sharp sword, and they should strike him with the single blow of one man. When they have killed him, his blood will be scattered among all the tribes, and I do not think the Banu Hashim will be able to fight all of Quraysh, and if they see that, they will accept the blood-money, so Quraysh will pay its diya, and we will be relieved." Iblis said: "This youth has spoken truly, and this is the best of your opinions; the saying is what he has said, I see no other."

So they dispersed upon Abu Jahl's proposal, though they were still gathered. Then Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that, and commanded him not to sleep on the bed where he usually slept. At that point Allah permitted him to leave for Medina. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, to sleep in his bed, and said: "Wrap yourself in my cloak, for no matter that you dislike will reach you."

Then the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, taking a handful of dust. Allah took their sight away from him, and he began scattering the dust over their heads while reciting: "We have placed shackles upon their necks, and they reach to the chins, so they are held up" [Ya-Sin: 8], and he went to the cave of Thawr, entered it with Abu Bakr, and left Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in Makkah to deliver the deposits (wada'i') that had been left with him, for the deposits used to be placed with him because of his truthfulness and trustworthiness. The polytheists were keeping watch over Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was on the bed of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), thinking that he was the Prophet. When morning came they rushed at him and saw that it was Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

Allah had turned back their plot, and there was not a single man of them but had dust placed upon his head.

They said: "Where is your companion?"

He said: "I do not know." So they followed his tracks and sent men in pursuit of him. When they reached the mountain and passed the cave, they saw on its entrance a spider's web and said: "If he had entered here, there would not be a spider's web at its door." He remained there three days, then he came to Medina. That is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: "And when those who disbelieved plotted against you to confine you" [[See Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/315, and Tarikh al-Tabari: 2/97–99.]].

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Muqsim and al-Suddi said: "to confine you" (liyuthbitūka) means "to bind you." Qatadah said: "to shackle you with chains."

Ata' and Abd Allah ibn Kathir said: "to imprison you." Aban ibn Tha'lab and Abu Hatim said: "to wound you with injuries and blows." And he recited:

I said: "Woe to you! What is in your document?" They said: "The caliph has become afflicted with an ailment."

[[Ibn Kathir attributed it in al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 8/153 to Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah.]]

It was also said: its meaning is "to mock you."

Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ata', from Ubayd ibn Umayr, from Abd al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah, that Abu Talib said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you know what your people are plotting against you?"

He said: "Yes, [they intend] to mock me and kill me or expel me." He said: "Who told you this?"

He said: "My Lord."

He said: "What a fine Lord your Lord is. So enjoin upon your Lord what is good."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I enjoin Him? Rather, He enjoins me to do good." [231] [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/299, and Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/314.]]

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "liyubayyitūka" (to attack you by night), from al-bayat. "Or they kill you or expel you. And they plot, and Allah plots. And Allah is the best of planners." Al-Hasan said: "They say, and Allah says." Al-Dahhak said: "They devise, and Allah devises." "Allah is the best of planners": He is the best of those who rescued you from them and destroyed them.

"And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, meaning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: 'We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this.'" That is because he used to travel as a merchant to Persia and al-Hirah, hearing the rhymed prose of their people and their accounts of the Persians and other nations. He passed by the Jews and Christians and saw them reading the Torah and the Gospel, bowing and prostrating. Then he came to Makkah and found Muhammad reciting the Qur'an and praying. So al-Nadr said: "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the myths of the ancients," meaning the reports of past nations and their lifespans.

Al-Suddi said: "Asajī' (fables) of the people of al-Hirah."

Al-asatir is the plural of a plural, and its root is from the verb "saṭara," meaning "he wrote." Its singular is "saṭr," then the plural "asṭār" or "suṭūr," then these two combine into "asāṭir" and "asāṭīr." It was also said: the singular of al-asatir is "usṭūrah" and "usṭār."

The few-plural is "asṭur."
